title: Exam 4 Practice Exam
description: Exam 4 practice, weighted like the professor's blueprint: 60 questions on ethics and law, leadership, teamwork, teaching and learning, and abbreviations and math, with one short case study and at least one ice chip question.

student.intro: A nurse on a medical-surgical unit is precepting a nursing student during a short-staffed day shift.

tabs.title: Unit Notes
tabs.html:
Unit Notes

0700: Five RNs for 30 clients; six is usual. The nurse is assigned six clients and the student. The student's clinical instructor is on the unit, supervising four other students.

The school's rules for students: students give IV medications only with the instructor or the RN present, and don't take verbal or phone orders.

tabs.title: Nurses' Notes
tabs.html:
Nurses' Notes

0930: The student reports that the client in room 4, admitted with a blood glucose of 486 mg/dL, said he has been skipping his insulin at home to save money, and asked the student not to tell anyone. The student promised.

1015: The student reports giving the client in room 6 her 1000 IV antibiotic, cefazolin, alone, “because you were busy, and I've done it lots of times.” The dose and the rate match the prescription. The client in room 6 has no rash, itching, or trouble breathing, and her vital signs are unchanged from 0800.

discharge.intro: A nurse on a medical unit is preparing a client for discharge tomorrow.

tabs.title: Nurse's Notes
tabs.html:
Nurse's Notes

Day 3, 0900: 72-year-old client admitted with new type 2 diabetes; now prescribed basal insulin by pen once daily. Lives alone; daughter visits weekly. Wears glasses, which are at the bedside. Says, “I left school in eighth grade.” Slept poorly because of a noisy roommate; yawning and asks to rest. Blood glucose 168 mg/dL. Denies pain.

1400: Awake after a 2-hour nap and alert. Picks up the insulin pen from the tray and asks to hold it. Says, “I want to learn to do the shot so I can take care of myself.”

tabs.title: Teaching Plan
tabs.html:
Teaching Plan: insulin pen

By discharge, the client will:

  1. Prime the pen with 2 units and dial the prescribed dose.
  2. Inject into the abdomen and hold the needle in place for 10 seconds.
  3. Explain, in his own words, the signs of low blood glucose and what to do.

questions.stem: Before a family meeting about a client's care, a nurse sorts the statements the family made into values, facts, and opinions. Which statement is a value?
options: “Her oxygen saturation dropped to 82% last night.”
“Life should be preserved for as long as possible.”
“She seems to be giving up too easily.”
“Her daughter wants a second opinion.”
questions.rationale:
A value is a deeply held belief about the worth of something, and it shapes choices: “Life should be preserved for as long as possible.”

“Giving up too easily” isn't the right answer: it sounds like a belief, but it's one person's judgment of this client in this situation, an opinion. The oxygen saturation and the daughter's request are facts: anyone can check them.

Takeaway: Value: a belief about what matters. Fact: something anyone can check. Opinion: a judgment about this situation. Sort them out first when resolving an ethical conflict (values clarification).

questions.stem: A client who is alert and oriented tells the nurse, “I've decided to stop dialysis. I'm tired of feeling sick three days a week.” The client's family is upset. Which response should the nurse make?
options: “Would you consider staying on dialysis a while longer, for your family's sake?”
“Stopping dialysis isn't safe, so I'll ask your provider to explain the risks again.”
“Tell me more about what led you to this decision, and I'll let your provider know.”
“I'll ask the ethics committee to decide whether stopping dialysis is allowed.”
questions.rationale:
A competent client has the right to refuse treatment, even treatment that keeps them alive (autonomy). The nurse explores the client's reasons (symptoms that could be eased, depression, or wrong information may be behind it), respects the decision, and tells the provider.

Asking the client to stay on dialysis for the family's sake isn't the right answer: it sounds caring, but it pressures a competent adult with other people's values. Having the provider explain the risks again assumes the client didn't understand, and treats the decision as a mistake to correct. An ethics committee gives advice on hard cases; it doesn't decide, and it isn't a way to overrule a competent refusal.

Takeaway: Respect a competent client's refusal: explore the reasons, tell the provider, and document. Don't persuade, and don't hand the decision to someone else.

questions.stem: A client asks a nurse to come back after lunch to help write a letter to the client's grandson. The nurse's afternoon turns busy, but the nurse returns at 1:30 as planned and helps with the letter. Which ethical principle is the nurse upholding?
options: Beneficence
Veracity
Autonomy
Fidelity
questions.rationale:
Fidelity is faithfulness: keeping promises and commitments. The nurse said they'd come back, and did, even on a busy afternoon.

Beneficence isn't the right answer: helping with the letter is doing good, but what the question describes is the promise kept. Veracity is truthfulness, and autonomy is respecting the client's own decisions: neither is what the nurse's return shows.

Takeaway: Look at the action: keeping a promise is fidelity, telling the truth is veracity, doing good is beneficence, respecting a choice is autonomy, and fair sharing of care is justice.

questions.stem: A client's family asks the nurse not to tell the client that a biopsy showed cancer. That afternoon, before the provider has talked with the client, the client asks, “Are my biopsy results back? What did they show?” Which response should the nurse make?
options: “They aren't back yet, so let's wait until your provider comes by.”
“They're back. I'll ask your provider to come and go over them with you today.”
“They showed some abnormal cells, and your provider will explain what that means.”
“Your family asked me to let them talk with you about the results first.”
questions.rationale:
Veracity means being truthful. The results are back, so the nurse says so, and asks the provider, who shares a new diagnosis, to come and discuss them with the client today. The information belongs to the client, not the family.

Saying the results aren't back yet isn't the right answer: it honors the family and seems to protect the client, but it's a lie. Describing abnormal cells starts giving the diagnosis before the provider does. Saying the family wants to talk first puts them in charge of a competent client's own information.

Takeaway: Never deny or invent results. Say truthfully what you can, and get the provider to discuss a new diagnosis with the client.

questions.stem: A charge nurse has one telemetry bed left, and two clients in the emergency department are waiting for it. Which of the following is the best basis for deciding which client gets the bed?
options: Which client arrived in the emergency department first
Which client is likely to need the bed for the shorter time
Which client's condition most needs cardiac monitoring now
Which client's provider asked for the bed first
questions.rationale:
Justice means distributing care fairly: by need, whatever a client's insurance, status, or place in line. The client whose condition most needs monitoring gets the bed.

Arrival order isn't the right answer: “first come, first served” sounds fair, but care goes by need, as in triage. Choosing the shorter stay is an efficiency argument, and which provider asked first is about the order of the requests: neither says who needs the bed.

Takeaway: Justice: share care and resources by need (acuity), not by insurance, status, arrival, or who asks first.

questions.stem: A nurse receives a prescription for a dose that is twice the usual range for the client's age. The provider is known to be irritable when called. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Hold the dose, and call the provider to check it before giving it
Give the dose, since the provider is accountable for the prescription
Give half the dose, and document why the dose was reduced
Hold the dose, and ask about it when the provider makes rounds
questions.rationale:
Nonmaleficence means doing no harm: a dose that could hurt the client is questioned before it's given, and settled now, whatever the provider's mood.

Giving it because the provider is accountable isn't the right answer: the nurse who gives a drug is accountable for it too. Waiting for rounds has the right idea at the wrong time: the client goes without the medication, or gets it wrong, in the meantime. Changing the dose to half is outside the nurse's scope.

Takeaway: Do no harm: the nurse who gives a drug is accountable for it. Question an unsafe order before giving it, and right away.

questions.stem: A competent adult client declines a blood transfusion for religious reasons. Which actions should the nurse take?
options: Ask the client's spouse whether they will consent to the transfusion.
Make sure the client understands the risks of declining.
Plan to transfuse if the client loses consciousness in an emergency.
Tell the provider that the client declines the transfusion.
Record the refusal and the information the client was given.
Encourage the client to reconsider once the hemoglobin result is back.
questions.rationale:
A competent adult may refuse any treatment, including one that could save their life (autonomy and religious freedom). The nurse makes sure the refusal is informed, tells the provider, and documents the refusal and the teaching.

Planning to transfuse in an emergency isn't the right answer: emergencies allow implied consent, but implied consent only fills in when the client's wishes are unknown. Transfusing against a known, competent refusal is battery. The spouse can't consent for a competent adult, and encouraging the client to reconsider puts the team's values on the client.

Takeaway: A competent client's informed refusal stands, even in an emergency: make sure it's informed, tell the provider, and document.

questions.stem: An older adult client who has full decision-making capacity refuses to use a bed alarm, calling it humiliating. The client fell once at home last month. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Turn on the bed alarm, since preventing a fall comes before comfort
Ask the provider to prescribe the alarm so that the client must use it
Tell the charge nurse, and move the client to a room near the station
Ask what bothers the client about the alarm, and look for options together
questions.rationale:
The client has capacity, so autonomy applies, and the nurse also owes beneficence (preventing a fall). The first step is to assess: find out what bothers the client (the noise, feeling watched) and agree on a safe option the client accepts, like a low bed, hourly rounding, and the call light in reach.

Turning on the alarm because safety comes first isn't the right answer: overriding a competent client's refusal without even learning why isn't the first step, and dignity matters too. A prescription doesn't override a refusal. Telling the charge nurse and moving the client may come later, but acts before understanding the problem.

Takeaway: When autonomy and safety pull apart, assess first: learn why the client refuses, then find a safe option the client accepts.

questions.stem: A nurse notices that a coworker has slurred speech and smells of alcohol while preparing medications for clients. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Offer to give the coworker's medications for the rest of the shift
Talk with the coworker privately after the shift about getting help
Report what was seen to the charge nurse right away
Report the coworker to the state board of nursing before the shift ends
questions.rationale:
Nonmaleficence, and the Code's duty to protect clients from unsafe practice: the nurse reports suspected impairment right away, through the chain of command, so the coworker is taken out of client care now.

Offering to give the coworker's medications isn't the right answer: it feels kind and protects this shift's clients, but it hides the problem and leaves the coworker's other care, and later shifts, unsafe. Talking privately about help matters, but after the clients are safe. A board of nursing report may follow through the facility's process, but it doesn't remove the coworker from care today.

Takeaway: Suspected impairment: protect clients first by reporting to the charge nurse or supervisor at once. Support for the coworker comes after.

questions.stem: A nursing student asks how the ANA Code of Ethics for Nurses relates to the state's nurse practice act. Which statement by the nurse is accurate?
options: “The Code is a federal law, so it overrides the state's practice act.”
“The Code is a guide to ethical practice, and the practice act is the law.”
“The Code applies to ANA members, and the practice act to other nurses.”
“The Code sets each nurse's scope, and the practice act sets the standards.”
questions.rationale:
The ANA Code of Ethics sets the ethical standard for every nurse, in every setting, member or not, and guides ethical decisions. It isn't a law. The nurse practice act is a state law: it defines the scope of practice, and the board of nursing enforces it.

The members only choice isn't the right answer: the ANA is a membership organization, but its Code is the whole profession's. The Code isn't a federal law, and it's the practice act that sets scope: standards of care come from the ANA's scope and standards, the practice act, and facility policies.

Takeaway: Ethics is what a nurse should do (the Code, for every nurse). Law is what a nurse must do (the practice act).

questions.stem: At the end of a 12-hour shift, after handing off the clients, a nurse who slept poorly is asked to stay for another 8 hours because the unit is short-staffed. The nurse feels exhausted. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Accept the shift, since leaving a short-staffed unit is abandonment
Accept the shift, and ask a coworker to double-check high-alert drugs
Decline the shift, and explain that fatigue would make the care unsafe
Decline the shift, and report the unit's staffing to the board of nursing
questions.rationale:
The Code says nurses owe the same duties to themselves as to others, including their own health and safety (Provision 5), and an exhausted nurse puts clients at risk. Turning down extra hours after a handoff isn't abandonment.

The abandonment choice isn't the right answer: the unit is short, but abandonment is leaving an assignment already accepted without handing off to a qualified nurse. A double-check helps with one risk, but doesn't fix the fatigue. Staffing concerns go up the chain of command first, not straight to the board.

Takeaway: The duty to self is part of the Code. Declining extra hours when too tired to be safe isn't abandonment; leaving an accepted assignment without a handoff is.

questions.stem: A competent older adult client wants to go home after discharge. The client's adult children want the client moved to a nursing home, and ask the nurse to support them at the care conference. Which action by the nurse is best?
options: Help the client tell the children their own wishes at the meeting
Support the children's plan, since they will provide most of the care
Stay neutral, and let the client and the children work it out together
Ask the provider to decide where the client should live after discharge
questions.rationale:
The nurse's primary commitment is to the client (Provision 2), and advocacy means helping the client's wishes be heard, above all when others want something else. A competent client decides where to live; the team can still share its safety concerns and offer services at home.

Staying neutral isn't the right answer: it feels fair, but it leaves the client without an advocate. The children's help matters, but they don't decide for a competent parent, and neither does the provider.

Takeaway: When family and a competent client disagree, the nurse advocates for the client's own wishes.

questions.stem: A nurse sees that a coworker posted on a personal account, “Rough night with our ‘frequent flyer’ in room 12 again.” The post names no one. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Ask the coworker to limit the post so that just friends can see it
Remind the coworker to leave room numbers out of future posts
Comment on the post to remind staff that client names stay private
Report the post to the nurse manager as a possible privacy breach
questions.rationale:
A post can identify a client without a name: the room number, the nickname, the unit, and the date are enough for someone to know who it is. The nurse reports a possible breach of confidentiality through the chain of command, following the facility's policy.

Limiting the post to friends isn't the right answer. Privacy settings don't make a post private: friends can copy and share it. Leaving out the room number still leaves a post about a client, and a public comment draws more attention to it, while suggesting that only names matter.

Takeaway: Any detail that could identify a client makes a post a privacy breach, whatever the settings. Report it through the chain of command.

questions.stem: A nurse receives several requests from clients on a medical unit. Which requests should the nurse support?
options: A client asks for an itemized copy of the hospital bill.
A client asks to be seen by a different provider.
A client asks the nurse not to tell the provider about a fall in the bathroom.
A client asks to see a chaplain of the client's own faith.
A client asks the nurse to leave a refusal of care out of the chart.
A client asks how to make a formal complaint about the care.
questions.rationale:
Client rights include accurate billing, choosing their own providers, religious freedom, and voicing complaints and being heard. The nurse helps with each.

Keeping a fall from the provider isn't the right answer. It sounds like privacy, but confidentiality keeps information from people outside the care team, not from the team: a fall needs assessment, a report, and documentation. A refusal of care is documented too, since the record must be accurate and complete.

Takeaway: Client rights include privacy from outsiders, not secrets from the care team: safety events and refusals are shared with the team and documented.

questions.stem: A nurse is assigned to help with a scheduled procedure that conflicts with the nurse's deeply held moral beliefs. It isn't an emergency. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Tell the charge nurse, and care for the client until another nurse takes over
Take part in the procedure, since a nurse can't refuse an assigned task
Explain to the client why the nurse won't take part in the procedure
Tell the charge nurse, and leave the care to the next nurse who is free
questions.rationale:
A nurse may decline to take part in a procedure that violates their moral beliefs (conscientious objection), when it isn't an emergency, but must still keep the client safe: tell the charge nurse, and keep caring for the client until another nurse takes over.

Telling the charge nurse and leaving the care to whoever is free isn't the right answer: the nurse is right to speak up, but the client can't be left without a handoff. A nurse isn't required to take part in every assigned procedure, and explaining the objection to the client puts the nurse's values on the client.

Takeaway: A nurse may opt out of a procedure for moral reasons, outside emergencies, but must tell the charge nurse and keep the client cared for until the handoff.

questions.stem: During a vaccine shortage, a public health nurse helps plan to give the limited doses first to the groups in which they will prevent the most deaths. Which approach to ethics guides this plan?
options: Deontology
Utilitarianism
Casuistry
Ethics of care
questions.rationale:
Utilitarianism judges an action by its consequences: the greatest good for the greatest number, as in triage and sharing out scarce vaccines.

Deontology isn't the right answer. The nurse has a duty to the public, but deontology judges an action by duty and rules, whatever the outcome, and this plan is judged by its outcome: deaths prevented. Casuistry compares a case with similar past cases, and the ethics of care centers on relationships and each person's own story.

Takeaway: Deontology: duty and rules. Utilitarianism: the most good for the most people. Casuistry: similar cases. Ethics of care: relationships and context. Feminist ethics: power and inequity.

questions.stem: A nurse believes a client in severe pain after surgery needs a stronger pain plan. The provider has declined twice to change it, and the nurse leaves each shift feeling powerless and upset. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Accept the provider's decision, since the pain plan is the provider's call
Ask to care for other clients, so that the situation stops being upsetting
Report the provider's refusal to change the plan to the state medical board
Document the pain scores, and take the concern up the chain of command
questions.rationale:
This is moral distress: the nurse knows the right action but is blocked from taking it, here by the hierarchy. The way through is to speak up with data (the documented pain assessments) and use the chain of command: the charge nurse, then the nurse manager, and an ethics consultation if it's still unresolved.

Accepting the provider's call isn't the right answer: the provider prescribes, but advocacy (Provision 3) means speaking up for the client with assessment data. Asking for other clients eases the nurse's distress and leaves the client in pain. Going to the medical board skips the chain of command, and a disagreement over a pain plan isn't misconduct.

Takeaway: Moral distress: you know what's right but are blocked. Speak up with your assessment data, and use the chain of command.

questions.stem: A client's adult children disagree about continuing their father's life support. He has no advance directive, and the team and family can't reach agreement. Which statement should the nurse make about asking the ethics committee for help?
options: “The committee will review the case and give all of you its recommendations.”
“The committee will make a decision that the family and team must follow.”
“The attending provider has to be the one who asks for a consultation.”
“The committee reviews cases after a death to find out what went wrong.”
questions.rationale:
An ethics committee is a multidisciplinary group that reviews hard cases and advises: it recommends, it doesn't decide. Any member of the team, the client, or the family can ask for a consultation.

A decision the family must follow isn't the right answer: the committee's advice carries weight, but decisions stay with the client or the client's legal decision-maker. Asking isn't limited to the attending provider, and reviewing what went wrong after a death describes a quality review, like a root cause analysis.

Takeaway: Ethics committee: anyone can ask for a consultation; it reviews and recommends, and doesn't decide.

questions.stem: A client's family wants “everything done,” but the client's living will declines CPR. The nurse recognizes this as an ethical problem. Which step of the decision-making process should the nurse take next?
options: Examine the nurse's own values about life support
Name the problem, such as autonomy versus the family's wishes
Gather the facts, including the client's wishes and condition
List the possible courses of action and their likely results
questions.rationale:
The seven steps follow the nursing process: (1) ask whether it's an ethical problem, (2) gather the relevant information, (3) identify the ethical elements and examine your own values, (4) name the problem, (5) list the possible actions, (6) make and carry out a plan, and (7) evaluate it. After step 1 comes assessment: the facts, the client's wishes, who decides, and the laws and policies that apply.

Examining the nurse's own values isn't the right answer. Values clarification matters, but it's step 3: the facts come first. Naming the problem and listing actions come later still.

Takeaway: Ethical decisions follow the nursing process: assess (gather the facts) before naming the problem or planning.

questions.stem: A newly licensed nurse asks how to prepare for the ethical problems that come up on the unit. Which strategies should the nurse recommend?
options: Follow the lead of the most experienced nurse on the unit.
Clarify your own values and how they could affect your care.
Learn the Code of Ethics and the facility's related policies.
Set personal values aside, and avoid thinking about them at work.
Use a step-by-step process, as with the nursing process.
Ask for an ethics consultation when a case needs one.
questions.rationale:
Strategies that make ethical decisions better: values clarification (knowing your own values and how they could color your care), knowing the Code of Ethics and the facility's policies, using a step-by-step process, and asking for an ethics consultation when a case needs one.

Setting values aside isn't the right answer. It sounds neutral, but values can't be switched off: the strategy is to know them, so they don't steer care unnoticed. Following the most experienced nurse replaces the nurse's own reasoning with someone else's.

Takeaway: Better ethical decisions: know your own values, the Code, and the policies, use a step-by-step process, and ask for help (an ethics consultation) when a case needs it.

questions.stem: A client with advanced COPD understands the benefits of a pulmonary rehabilitation program but declines it, saying, “I'd rather spend my energy on my garden and my grandkids.” A nursing student says rehab would improve the client's quality of life. Which response by the nurse is best?
options: “Let's show the client how rehab could improve breathing and quality of life.”
“The client defines quality of life, so we support the plan the client chose.”
“Let's ask the family to encourage the client to try a few sessions first.”
“Let's chart the refusal as noncompliance so the provider can follow up.”
questions.rationale:
Quality of life is defined by the client, not the team. This client understands the benefits, has weighed them against what matters most to them, and has made an informed choice: the nurse supports it.

Showing how rehab helps isn't the right answer. Teaching is part of nursing, but the client already understands: more persuasion puts the team's values on the client. Asking the family to push adds pressure, and calling an informed refusal noncompliance labels the client's choice as a failure. The refusal is documented as a refusal.

Takeaway: The client defines their own quality of life. After an informed choice, support it: don't persuade, pressure, or label it.

questions.stem: A client who is dying of cancer is on a ventilator because the family insists on full treatment. The nurse believes the treatments only prolong the client's suffering, and feels distressed giving them. Which action by the nurse is best?
options: Tell the family that comfort care is what the nurse would choose
Ask the charge nurse to assign the client to another nurse
Keep giving the care, and keep the nurse's concerns to themselves
Ask for an ethics consultation to review the plan of care
questions.rationale:
The nurse is in moral distress: believing the care is wrong, but required to give it. An ethics consultation brings the team and family together to review the plan, and any team member can ask for one.

Keeping the concerns to themselves isn't the right answer: it seems professional, but unspoken moral distress leads to burnout, and the Code expects nurses to raise ethical concerns. Telling the family what the nurse would choose puts the nurse's values on them. Asking for another assignment eases the nurse's distress, but leaves the concern about the plan unspoken.

Takeaway: Moral distress over a plan of care: raise it, through an ethics consultation or the chain of command. Don't stay silent, and don't push your own values on the family.

questions.stem: A client's daughter tells the nurse, “Don't let Dad sign the consent for the feeding tube. He doesn't really understand it.” The client, who is alert, agreed to the procedure with the provider this morning. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Ask the client what he knows about the tube and what he wants
Tell the daughter that her father has the right to decide for himself
Tell the provider that the client's consent may not be valid
Ask the daughter to sign the consent form along with her father
questions.rationale:
In an ethical problem, the nurse assesses before acting. The daughter's concern may or may not be right, so the nurse first finds out from the client himself what he knows about the procedure and what he wants.

Telling the provider that consent may not be valid isn't the right answer: it's the right next step if the client can't explain the procedure, but it comes after the nurse checks. Telling the daughter he has the right to decide is true for a competent client, but answers before anyone knows whether he understood. The daughter's signature adds nothing: a competent adult consents for himself.

Takeaway: When a concern is raised about a decision, assess first: hear from the client before acting on what others say.

questions.stem: A nurse asks where the state's rule on how many continuing education hours a nurse needs to renew a license comes from. The board of nursing wrote the rule under the state's nurse practice act. Which type of law is the rule?
options: Constitutional law
Statutory law
Administrative law
Common law
questions.rationale:
Administrative (regulatory) law is made of the rules that government agencies write, like the board of nursing's rules on license renewal, or the rules of the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services.

Statutory law isn't the right answer: the rule comes under the nurse practice act, which is a statute, but the legislature passes the act, and the detailed rules the board writes under it are administrative law. Constitutional law comes from the federal and state constitutions, like the right to privacy, and common law comes from earlier court decisions.

Takeaway: Statutes are passed by legislatures (the nurse practice act, HIPAA). Agencies' rules are administrative law (the board of nursing's rules). Court decisions are common law.

questions.stem: A clinic's new policy says its RNs may diagnose strep throat and start antibiotics when the provider is busy. The state's nurse practice act doesn't include diagnosing or prescribing in RN practice. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Follow the practice act, and raise the policy with the nurse manager
Follow the clinic's policy, since the clinic is accountable for its policies
Follow the policy until the board of nursing rules on the conflict
Follow the policy, and tell the nurse manager about any concerns
questions.rationale:
The nurse practice act, a state law, sets the scope of practice, and a facility's policy can't stretch it. When the two conflict, the nurse follows the stricter one, here the law, and raises the conflict with the nurse manager.

Following the clinic's policy isn't the right answer: nurses are expected to follow policy, but a policy can't authorize what the law doesn't, and it's the nurse's own license at risk. Following it until the board rules, or while telling the manager about concerns, still means diagnosing and prescribing outside the RN scope.

Takeaway: A facility policy can narrow a nurse's scope but can't widen it past the practice act. When they conflict, follow the stricter one, and raise the conflict.

questions.stem: A nurse inserts a urinary catheter, a skill within the RN scope, but skips the sterile steps of the facility's procedure. The client develops a urinary tract infection. Which statement about the nurse's legal position is accurate?
options: The skill is within the RN scope, so the nurse met the legal standard.
The facility, not the nurse, is liable when its procedure isn't followed.
No law was broken, so the client can't bring a case against the nurse.
The nurse was within scope, but can be found below the standard of care.
questions.rationale:
Scope says what a nurse may do. Standards of care say how well it must be done: the knowledge and skill nurses ordinarily use, drawn from the ANA's standards, the practice act, facility policies, and accreditation standards. A task within scope, done below the standard, can be negligence.

Meeting the legal standard because the skill is in scope isn't the right answer: it mixes up the two ideas. The facility may share liability, but nurses are accountable for their own actions. And a client can bring a civil case for harm without any criminal law being broken.

Takeaway: Scope: what a nurse may do. Standards: how well it must be done. Doing an in-scope task below the standard can still be negligence.

questions.stem: At the start of a shift, a nurse realizes that their license expired two days ago, because the renewal was never submitted. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Tell the nurse manager, and work while the renewal is processed
Tell the nurse manager, and don't work until the renewal is complete
Work the shift under the direct supervision of the charge nurse
Work the shift, but leave the medication tasks to another nurse
questions.rationale:
Practicing with an expired license is practicing without a license, which the nurse practice act forbids. The nurse tells the manager and doesn't work until the renewal is complete.

Working under the charge nurse's supervision isn't the right answer: students practice under supervision, but supervision doesn't make a nurse licensed. Telling the manager but working while the renewal is processed is still working unlicensed, and leaving out medication tasks doesn't help: any nursing care counts as practice.

Takeaway: No active license, no nursing practice: report it and don't work until the license is renewed. The board of nursing can deny, suspend, or revoke a license.

questions.stem: A client without health insurance comes to a private hospital's emergency department with chest pain. The registration clerk suggests sending the client to the county hospital across town. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Arrange the transfer, since the county hospital serves uninsured clients
Make sure the client is screened and stabilized at this hospital
Ask the social worker to find coverage before the client is examined
Have the client sign a form accepting the costs before the exam
questions.rationale:
EMTALA requires every emergency department to give a screening exam and stabilize an emergency, whatever the client can pay, and it forbids transferring an unstable client from a private hospital to a public one for financial reasons.

Calling the social worker isn't the right answer: a social worker is the right first call for a client without insurance in most situations, but in an emergency, payment questions can't delay the exam. A transfer for lack of insurance is what EMTALA forbids, and asking the client to accept the costs first delays care in the same way.

Takeaway: EMTALA: screen and stabilize every emergency, whatever the client can pay. Coverage questions come after, never before.

questions.stem: During an admission interview, a client says, “I don't have a living will or anything like that.” Which action should the nurse take?
options: Tell the client that an advance directive is needed before discharge
Ask the client's next of kin to help fill one out for the client
Ask the provider to bring up advance directives at the next visit
Give the client written information about advance directives
questions.rationale:
The Patient Self-Determination Act requires facilities to give clients written information on admission about their right to make decisions about their care, to refuse treatment, and to make an advance directive. The nurse gives the information and documents whether the client has one.

Leaving it to the provider at the next visit isn't the right answer: providers discuss goals of care, but the law asks for the information at admission, and the nurse can give it now. An advance directive is the client's choice, so it isn't required before discharge, and next of kin can't make one for a client.

Takeaway: Patient Self-Determination Act: on admission, ask about an advance directive, give written information, and document. Having one is the client's choice.

questions.stem: A client dies in the intensive care unit. The client hadn't registered as an organ donor and left no instructions about donation. Who may give consent to donate the client's organs?
options: The client's family, such as the spouse or adult children
The attending provider, who pronounced the death
The hospital's ethics committee, after a review
No one, since the client didn't register as a donor
questions.rationale:
The Uniform Anatomical Gift Act is the basis of the organ donation system. Competent adults can choose to donate, and when a person dies without having decided either way, the family can consent to donation. (The Uniform Determination of Death Act defines death: the irreversible end of breathing and circulation, or of all brain function, including the brainstem.)

No one isn't the right answer: registering is how adults say yes, but when the client made no choice, the family can make it. The provider pronounces death but doesn't consent to donation, and an ethics committee advises rather than consents.

Takeaway: Uniform Anatomical Gift Act: adults can choose to donate, and if they didn't decide, the family can consent after death.

questions.stem: A nurse is caring for clients on a surgical unit. Which actions should the nurse take to protect the clients' health information?
options: Log off the electronic record before leaving the workstation.
Read the client's lab results to the client's sister when she calls.
Check a hospitalized neighbor's chart to see how the neighbor is doing.
Share the client's diet orders and allergies with the dietitian.
Give updates by phone to callers who give the client's passcode.
Talk about the client's care with a coworker over lunch in the cafeteria.
questions.rationale:
Protecting health information means logging off, sharing the minimum necessary with the people directly involved in care (the dietitian needs the diet orders and allergies), and giving phone updates only to people the client authorized, like those with the passcode.

Checking a neighbor's chart isn't the right answer: it comes from caring, but looking at any chart without a role in that client's care is a violation. The sister hasn't been authorized, and a cafeteria is a public place, however quietly the nurses talk.

Takeaway: Minimum necessary, to people directly involved in care or authorized by the client. A caring reason doesn't make an unauthorized look at a chart acceptable.

questions.stem: A client who is deaf and uses American Sign Language is admitted for surgery tomorrow. Which action should the nurse take for the preoperative teaching?
options: Ask the client's hearing daughter to interpret the teaching
Write out the teaching, and have the client read it
Arrange for a qualified medical interpreter who uses ASL
Speak slowly while facing the client, so the client can lip-read
questions.rationale:
The Americans with Disabilities Act requires reasonable accommodations, and for a client who uses ASL that means a qualified medical interpreter, for teaching and for consent.

The daughter isn't the right answer: she's fluent and there, but family members may leave out or change information, and the client loses privacy. ASL is its own language, so written English may not be understood fully, and lip-reading catches only part of what's said.

Takeaway: ADA: reasonable accommodations, like a qualified interpreter. Not family, not lip-reading, and not just written notes.

questions.stem: Driving home from a shift, a nurse stops at a car crash where a driver is bleeding heavily from a leg wound. A bystander has called 911. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Apply direct pressure, and stay until the paramedics take over
Apply direct pressure, then leave once a bystander can hold it
Give first aid, and accept the driver's offer to pay for the help
Wait for the paramedics, since giving aid could create legal liability
questions.rationale:
Good Samaritan laws limit the liability of a nurse who helps at an emergency scene in good faith, without pay, within their training, and without gross negligence. Once the nurse starts, the nurse stays until someone with equal or more training takes over.

Leaving once a bystander can hold the pressure isn't the right answer: the bleeding is controlled, but a bystander has less training, so leaving abandons the driver. Accepting pay can remove the law's protection, and waiting for fear of liability is the worry these laws exist to ease.

Takeaway: Good Samaritan: help in good faith, within your training, without pay, and stay until someone with equal or more training takes over.

questions.stem: A nurse in an emergency department is caring for several clients. In which situations should the nurse share information without the client's consent, following the state's reporting laws?
options: A client who says they used cocaine before the crash
A client with a gunshot wound to the thigh
A 4-year-old with burns that don't fit the parent's story
A client who leaves the department against medical advice
A client with a new diagnosis of active tuberculosis
questions.rationale:
Confidentiality has exceptions set by law: mandatory reports like gunshot wounds, suspected abuse (burns that don't match the story), and certain communicable diseases, like tuberculosis, to public health. A court order and a duty to warn are exceptions too.

Cocaine use isn't the right answer: it's illegal, but a client's report of drug use is protected health information, not something the nurse reports to the police. A client who leaves against medical advice signs a form when possible, and the nurse documents and tells the provider; it isn't reported outside the facility.

Takeaway: Share without consent only when the law requires it: mandatory reports (abuse, gunshot wounds, reportable diseases), a court order, or a duty to warn.

questions.stem: A nurse brings a surgical consent form to a client to sign. The client asks, “Will they be taking out my whole colon, or just part of it?” Which action should the nurse take?
options: Explain the surgery, using the consent form's description
Have the client sign, and tell the surgeon about the question
Hold off on signing, and ask the surgeon to talk with the client
Ask the charge nurse to answer the question before the client signs
questions.rationale:
The provider explains the procedure and obtains consent. The nurse witnesses the signature, confirming that the client signs voluntarily, appears competent, and understands. A question about what will be removed shows the client doesn't fully understand, so the nurse stops and asks the surgeon to explain.

Explaining from the form isn't the right answer: the nurse may know the answer, but explaining the procedure for consent is the surgeon's duty. Signing first means signing without understanding, and the charge nurse isn't the one doing the surgery either.

Takeaway: The provider explains and obtains consent; the nurse witnesses. Questions or confusion: stop, and call the provider.

questions.stem: A client received IV morphine for pain 20 minutes ago and is drowsy. The surgeon now asks the nurse to witness the client's signature on the surgical consent. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Witness the signature, since the surgeon has explained the procedure
Have the client sign, and note the morphine's time on the form
Ask the client's spouse to sign the consent in the client's place
Tell the surgeon about the morphine, since consent now may not be valid
questions.rationale:
Valid consent needs capacity: an alert client who isn't under the effect of opioids or sedatives. That's why consent is signed before preoperative medications. The nurse tells the surgeon, so the signing can wait until the client is alert.

Witnessing because the surgeon explained isn't the right answer: the witness confirms the client can understand now, and a drowsy client can't. Noting the morphine's time documents the problem without fixing it, and the spouse doesn't sign for a client who will soon be able to decide for themselves.

Takeaway: Consent needs capacity: get it before opioids or sedatives. If they've been given, tell the provider and wait.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old client who is married comes to an urgent care clinic with a broken wrist. Who should the nurse ask to sign the consent for treatment?
options: The client's parent, since the client is under 18
The client, since being married lets the client consent
The client's spouse, since a spouse consents for a married minor
The provider, since a fracture needs treatment right away
questions.rationale:
A parent or guardian usually consents for a minor, but emancipated minors, such as those who are married, in the military, or self-supporting, consent for themselves (states add their own exceptions).

The parent isn't the right answer: the client is under 18, but marriage emancipates the client. A spouse doesn't consent for a competent client, and a broken wrist isn't the kind of emergency in which consent is implied: that's for a threat to life when no one is available to consent.

Takeaway: Minors: a parent or guardian consents, except emancipated minors (married, military, self-supporting) and the state's own exceptions.

questions.stem: A client with end-stage heart failure has a DNR order and develops pneumonia. Which actions should the nurse take?
options: Give the antibiotics the provider prescribed.
Stop taking routine vital signs, since the order limits care.
Start CPR if the heart stops and the family asks for it.
Ask the provider to cancel the DNR so the pneumonia can be treated.
Give oxygen to ease the client's shortness of breath.
Keep giving pain medication and comfort measures.
questions.rationale:
A DNR order means no CPR if the heart or breathing stops. It doesn't mean “do not treat”: the client still gets the antibiotics, oxygen, pain medication, comfort measures, and monitoring the care plan calls for.

Canceling the DNR so the pneumonia can be treated isn't the right answer: it treats DNR as “no treatment,” but nothing in the order stops the pneumonia treatment. Stopping vital signs makes the same mistake. The order stands if the heart stops, and the family can't override the client's decision.

Takeaway: DNR means no CPR, not no care: keep treating, monitoring, and comforting the client.

questions.stem: A client's living will declines mechanical ventilation. The client, who is alert and oriented, now tells the nurse, “I've changed my mind. If I need a breathing machine, I want it.” Which action should the nurse take?
options: Follow the living will, since it was signed and witnessed
Ask the client's health care proxy to confirm the change
Ask the ethics committee which of the wishes to follow
Tell the provider, and help the client update the directive
questions.rationale:
A competent client can change or revoke an advance directive at any time, and the client's current wishes come first. The nurse tells the provider, helps the client update the directive, and documents.

Following the signed living will isn't the right answer: it's a legal document, but it speaks for the client only when the client can't speak. A health care proxy decides only when the client can't, and an ethics committee isn't needed when a competent client states their wishes.

Takeaway: Advance directives apply when the client can't decide. A competent client's current wishes win, and the client can change the directive at any time.

questions.stem: A client whose durable power of attorney for health care names a close friend is unconscious after a stroke. The client's spouse disagrees with the friend about placing a feeding tube. Whose decision should the nurse follow?
options: The person the client named as health care proxy
The client's spouse, since a spouse is the legal next of kin
The provider, since the client can no longer decide
The client's adult children, together with the spouse
questions.rationale:
A durable power of attorney for health care names the person who decides when the client can't: the health care proxy, who follows the client's known wishes. The client chose the friend.

The spouse isn't the right answer: next of kin often decide when no one is named, but a named proxy comes first. The provider advises but doesn't make the client's choices, and the adult children don't outrank a proxy the client named.

Takeaway: Durable power of attorney for health care: the named proxy decides when the client can't, ahead of family. Living will: written instructions.

questions.stem: A competent client admitted with chest pain, whose tests aren't finished, tells the nurse, “I'm leaving now. I've waited long enough.” Which action should the nurse take?
options: Stand in the doorway until the provider can talk with the client
Tell the provider, and ask the client to sign the AMA form
Ask security to keep the client on the unit until the tests are done
Give the prescribed lorazepam so that the client will stay for the tests
questions.rationale:
A competent client may leave against medical advice. The nurse tells the provider, explains the risks, asks the client to sign the AMA form, and documents. Keeping the client from leaving is false imprisonment.

Standing in the doorway until the provider comes isn't the right answer: it seems to buy time for a talk, but blocking a competent client is detaining them without legal cause. So is having security hold the client, and giving a sedative to keep the client in place.

Takeaway: False imprisonment: restraining or detaining without legal cause, by blocking, holding, restraints without a prescription, or sedation. A competent client may leave AMA.

questions.stem: A nurse tells a client who refuses an oral medication, “If you won't swallow it, I'll have to put it down a tube.” The nurse doesn't touch the client. Which tort does the nurse's statement represent?
options: Assault
Battery
False imprisonment
Invasion of privacy
questions.rationale:
Assault is a threat, or an attempt to touch, that makes a person fear harmful contact. No touching is needed: the words alone can be assault.

Battery isn't the right answer: the threat is about forced treatment, but battery needs contact without consent, and nothing touched the client. False imprisonment is detaining without legal cause, and invasion of privacy is exposing private information.

Takeaway: Assault = a threat (no touch). Battery = body contact without consent. Slander = spoken. Libel = written.

questions.stem: A nurse gives a client's scheduled insulin without checking the blood glucose first, as the policy requires. The client's glucose stays in the normal range, and the client has no ill effects. Which element of malpractice would a claim against the nurse lack?
options: Duty to the client
Breach of the standard of care
Foreseeability of harm
Harm to the client
questions.rationale:
Malpractice needs every element: duty, breach, foreseeability, causation, harm, and damages. The nurse had a duty to the client, skipping a required check breached the standard, and low blood glucose after insulin is foreseeable, but there was no harm.

Breach isn't the right answer: nothing went wrong, but skipping a required check is a breach whatever the outcome. Without harm there's no malpractice claim, but the error is still reported.

Takeaway: Malpractice needs duty, breach, foreseeability, causation, harm, and damages. A breach without harm isn't malpractice, but it's still an error to report.

questions.stem: A nurse manager is reviewing events on the unit. Which actions by staff could lead to a claim of an intentional or quasi-intentional tort?
options: Applying wrist restraints to a calm client without a prescription
Charting a client's exact words when the client swore at staff
Giving a flu shot to a client after the client said no
Telling other staff that a coworker “is always high,” with no facts
Holding a client's arm to steady the client, after the client agreed
Leaving a client's record open on a screen in the hallway
questions.rationale:
Restraints without a prescription are false imprisonment, a shot the client refused is battery, a damaging spoken claim with no facts is slander (defamation), and leaving a record open is invasion of privacy.

Charting the client's exact words isn't the right answer: swearing sounds harmful to put in a record, but quoting what a client said is objective documentation, not defamation. Touching a client who agreed isn't battery: battery is touching without consent.

Takeaway: Intentional torts: assault, battery, false imprisonment. Quasi-intentional: invasion of privacy and defamation (slander spoken, libel written). Consent and objective facts are the defenses.

questions.stem: A postoperative client's blood pressure has dropped from 128/80 to 92/58 over 2 hours, and the client is restless. The nurse called the provider 30 minutes ago, and the provider hasn't called back. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Document the readings, and wait for the provider to call back
Recheck the blood pressure in 1 hour, and call again if it falls
Notify the charge nurse, and use the chain of command to get help
Report the provider's delay to the nurse manager after the shift
questions.rationale:
A client getting worse needs care now. When the provider doesn't respond, the nurse uses the chain of command, starting with the charge nurse. Failing to report worsening findings, or to keep going until someone acts, is a classic example of negligence.

Waiting for the call back isn't the right answer: the nurse has already called, but the duty to the client continues until someone acts. Rechecking in 1 hour loses time a falling blood pressure may not allow, and reporting the delay after the shift deals with the provider, not with the client who needs help now.

Takeaway: Worsening client, no response: go up the chain of command. Documenting and waiting can be negligence.

questions.stem: A nurse notices that a coworker charts hourly rounds on clients that weren't done, saying, “Everyone does it, and the unit gets graded on it.” Which action should the nurse take?
options: Remind the coworker to chart rounds after doing them, from now on
Do the coworker's missed rounds so that the clients are checked
Ask the coworker to fix the earlier entries with late entries
Report it to the nurse manager or the compliance hotline
questions.rationale:
Charting care that wasn't given is falsifying records, a form of fraud (intentional deception for gain), and it can hide harm to clients. The nurse reports it through the chain of command or the compliance hotline. Whistleblowers are protected.

Reminding the coworker isn't the right answer: it feels collegial, but it leaves the false entries in place and the practice unreported. Doing the missed rounds helps today's clients but hides the problem, and late entries can't make up care that never happened.

Takeaway: Fraud is intentional deception (billing or charting care never given). Waste is overuse; abuse is improper practice that adds cost. Report suspected fraud through the chain of command or the hotline.

questions.stem: Which actions should the nurse take about the IV antibiotic the student gave in room 6?
options: Check the client in room 6 for a reaction, and check the IV line and site
Report the student to the state board of nursing
Tell the clinical instructor what the student did
Hold the client's next antibiotic dose until the provider has been told
Complete an incident report, following the facility's policy
Wait until the end of the shift to tell the instructor, so the student stays calm
questions.rationale:
The client comes first: check her for a reaction, and check the line and site. The student went beyond what the school allows, so the nurse tells the clinical instructor now, and completes an incident report as policy requires, since a rule was broken even though no harm is seen. Students are accountable for their own actions; the nurse is accountable for the client.

Waiting until the end of the shift isn't the right answer: it spares the student for now, but the instructor supervises the student today and needs to know before the student gives anything else. A student isn't licensed, so the school, not the board of nursing, deals with the student. The dose and rate were right and the client is stable, so holding the next dose would delay her treatment for no reason.

Takeaway: When a student goes beyond the rules: the client first, then the instructor and an incident report, right away.

questions.stem: Which response by the nurse to the student about the client in room 4 is best?
options: “You promised him, so keep it to yourself. Breaking his trust could stop him from telling us things.”
“Tell the provider yourself, and leave him out of it so he doesn't feel that you betrayed him.”
“His team needs to know, since it affects his safety. Let's talk with him together about why.”
“Let's wait and see if he brings it up with his provider before we decide what to do about it.”
questions.rationale:
Skipping insulin to save money affects the client's safety, his diabetes plan, and his discharge, so his care team needs to know. Confidentiality keeps information within the team, not from it. Talking with the client together explains why it's shared and keeps his trust, and the team can look for help with the cost.

Keeping the promise isn't the right answer: fidelity is a real principle, but a promise of secrecy can't outweigh a client's safety, which is why nurses don't make one. Going around the client gets the information to the provider, but damages his trust when he finds out, and waiting leaves a dangerous gap in his plan.

Takeaway: Confidentiality means within the care team, not a secret from it. Explain to the client why it's shared, with him, not behind his back.

questions.stem: A nurse won't tell a worried client a small lie to calm them, saying, “Lying is wrong, whatever good it might do.” Which approach to ethics is the nurse following?
options: Utilitarianism, which judges an act by its outcome for the most people
Casuistry, which compares the situation with similar earlier cases
Deontology, which judges an act by duties and rules
Beneficence, which weighs what will do the client the most good
questions.rationale:
Deontology judges an act by whether it follows a duty or rule (“lying is wrong”), whatever the consequences. The nurse's reason is the rule itself, not the result.

Utilitarianism isn't the right answer: the lie might seem to help, but utilitarianism weighs outcomes; this nurse refuses despite the good outcome. Beneficence is a principle, not an approach.

Takeaway: Deontology: duty and rules. Utilitarianism: the greatest good. Casuistry: compare similar cases.

questions.stem: An ethics committee is deciding whether to stop a client's feeding tube. A member suggests reviewing how the committee decided three similar cases in the past. Which approach to ethics is the member suggesting?
options: Deontology
Casuistry
Utilitarianism
Veracity
questions.rationale:
Casuistry is case-based reasoning: it compares the current situation with similar earlier cases and how they were decided, then applies what fits.

Deontology isn't the right answer: committees follow rules, but deontology applies duties and rules directly, not earlier cases. Veracity is a principle (truth-telling), not an approach.

Takeaway: Casuistry = reasoning from similar cases.

questions.stem: A nurse educator is reviewing professional values. For each action, click to specify the value it shows.
rows: A nurse reports a medication error she made, though no one saw it
A nurse stays after her shift to support a dying client's family
A nurse speaks at a town meeting for a free clinic for uninsured residents
A nurse admits not knowing how to use a new pump and asks for help
A nurse volunteers at a homeless shelter on weekends
questions.rationale:
Altruism is concern for others' welfare, putting their needs first (staying with a family, volunteering). Integrity is acting honestly and by the code even when no one is watching (reporting one's own error, admitting what one doesn't know). Social justice is working for fair treatment and access to care for everyone (a free clinic for uninsured people).

Calling the free clinic altruism is a mistake, even though it helps others. It's about fair access for a whole group, which is social justice.

Takeaway: Altruism: others first. Integrity: honest and by the code. Social justice: fairness and access for all.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing federal laws. For each situation, click to specify the law that applies.
rows: A client with diabetes can't be denied health insurance because of the condition
A hospital must tell clients when a data breach exposed their electronic records
A client's record can't be shared with the client's employer without permission
An emergency department must screen and stabilize a woman in labor, whether or not she can pay
A 24-year-old can stay on a parent's health insurance plan
questions.rationale:
The Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act (PPACA) expanded coverage: no denial for preexisting conditions, and young adults can stay on a parent's plan until 26. The HITECH Act promoted electronic health records and strengthened HIPAA's rules, including telling clients about breaches. HIPAA protects the privacy of health information. EMTALA requires emergency screening and stabilization regardless of ability to pay.

Giving the data breach to HIPAA is a mistake, even though it's about privacy. The breach-notification rule for electronic records came with the HITECH Act, which built on HIPAA.

Takeaway: PPACA: coverage. HITECH: electronic records and breaches. HIPAA: privacy. EMTALA: emergency care for all.

questions.stem: A hospital names a staff nurse the new unit manager, with authority over scheduling, budgets, and hiring. A coworker asks what the new role means for the unit. Which statement by the charge nurse is accurate?
options: “She now holds a formal position, and she'll still need influence to lead us.”
“Her title gives her influence, so staff will follow her plans without persuasion.”
“She's now an informal leader, since her authority comes from her peers.”
“Managing is her job now, so leading the unit falls to the senior staff.”
questions.rationale:
A manager holds an official position in the organization, so management is always formal. Leadership is different: it's the use of interpersonal skills to influence others toward a goal. A new manager has authority, but still has to earn the staff's cooperation by leading.

“Her title gives her influence” isn't the right answer: authority and influence sound alike, but a title gives the right to direct, not the willingness to follow. An informal leader has no official appointment, which isn't the case here. And managing doesn't hand leading to someone else: every nurse, manager or not, is expected to lead.

Takeaway: Management is a formal position; leadership is influence. A good manager needs both.

questions.stem: During a busy night, a staff nurse with no charge role notices a new nurse falling behind, rallies two coworkers to help, and the unit runs smoothly. Coworkers often go to this nurse for advice. Which explanation fits this nurse's role best?
options: A formal leader acting on authority from the unit
A manager carrying out the organizing function for the shift
An informal leader whose influence comes from peers' trust
A charge nurse acting through the chain of command
questions.rationale:
An informal leader isn't appointed to direct others but takes on a leadership role because of who they are: coworkers trust the nurse, ask for advice, and follow when the nurse rallies them.

A manager organizing resources isn't the right answer, even though the nurse did move people to where help was needed. But organizing is a management function, and management is always formal: this nurse holds no official position. A formal leader and a charge nurse both have official authority, which the stem rules out.

Takeaway: No title, but peers follow: that's an informal leader, leading by influence.

questions.stem: A nurse educator teaches a group of new graduate nurses about leadership and management. Which statement by a new graduate indicates an understanding of the teaching?
options: “I'll start building leadership skills once I'm ready for a charge role.”
“I'll lead and manage every shift, starting with my own clients' care.”
“A strong manager becomes a strong leader once the title brings respect.”
“My influence on the team will come mostly from my job title.”
questions.rationale:
All nurses manage and lead in practice: they manage their own clients' care, time, and resources, and they influence coworkers, clients, and families. So every nurse should keep building both skills from the first day.

Waiting for a charge role isn't the right answer, even though leadership sounds like a job title. But leadership doesn't wait for a position. The other two choices tie influence to a title, which mixes up authority (from the position) with influence (from interpersonal skills).

Takeaway: Every nurse leads and manages, starting with their own clients; influence comes from skills, not a title.

questions.stem: A nurse manager and a respected staff nurse both want to shorten call-light response times on their unit. Which action should the nurse manager take, since it needs the manager's formal authority?
options: Share a vision of faster responses with coworkers
Model answering call lights promptly on each shift
Persuade peers to try a no-pass zone for call lights
Change the unit's assignments to add a float aide
questions.rationale:
Changing staff assignments and adding staff means directing others' work and assigning resources, which takes the authority of an official position: that's management.

Sharing a vision isn't the right answer, even though managers do share visions. But a vision, role modeling, and persuasion are tools of leadership, and an informal leader can use all three without any title.

Takeaway: Influence (vision, example, persuasion) is open to any nurse; directing staff and resources takes a manager's formal authority.

questions.stem: A nurse manager is choosing a staff nurse to lead a falls-prevention project, and wants someone coworkers already follow. Which observations should the manager weigh in favor of a staff nurse?
options: Coworkers ask the nurse for advice on difficult cases.
The nurse has more years on the unit than anyone else.
Peers began a bedside safety check after the nurse modeled it.
The nurse explains goals in ways coworkers understand and accept.
The nurse holds the highest certification on the unit.
The nurse follows unit policies closely and rarely needs reminders.
questions.rationale:
Coworkers following a nurse is a sign of influence, the heart of leadership: peers ask the nurse for advice, copy what the nurse models, and accept the goals the nurse explains. An effective leader turns a vision into goals others understand, and acts as a role model.

Following policy closely isn't the right answer: it makes a reliable employee, but complying isn't the same as influencing others. Seniority and certification are worth respecting, but neither one shows that coworkers follow this nurse.

Takeaway: Look for influence (peers seek the nurse out, copy the nurse, accept the nurse's goals), not years, credentials, or compliance.

questions.stem: A nurse manager notices that staff follow a new hourly rounding policy only on the days she's on the unit. Which change in the manager's approach is most likely to make the practice last?
options: Explain why rounding matters and let nurses shape how it's done
Post the policy in the break room and audit rounding each week
Assign one nurse each shift to remind coworkers about rounding
Add rounding to each nurse's annual evaluation so it affects raises
questions.rationale:
Staff comply when the manager is watching because the policy rests on authority alone. Lasting change comes from leadership: a vision staff understand, and a say in how it's carried out, so they own the practice.

Weekly audits aren't the right answer, even though measuring is a real management function (controlling), and it can show the problem. But audits and evaluations tied to raises keep the practice tied to being watched or rewarded, and a reminder nurse just moves the watching to a coworker.

Takeaway: Authority gets compliance while someone's watching; vision and participation get commitment.

questions.stem: A charge nurse lets an experienced, motivated team decide among themselves how to divide the day's work, and checks in only when someone asks. Which leadership style is the charge nurse using?
options: Democratic
Laissez-faire
Bureaucratic
Situational
questions.rationale:
A laissez-faire leader takes a hands-off approach and lets the group decide based on its own expertise. It can work when the group is made up of committed, skilled members, like this team.

Democratic isn't the right answer, even though the team does decide. But a democratic leader stays involved: the leader encourages discussion and coordinates the group's decision. A bureaucratic leader leads by the rules and procedures, and a situational leader adapts the style to each situation.

Takeaway: Hands-off, the group decides alone: laissez-faire. The leader guides a group decision: democratic.

questions.stem: A charge nurse usually asks for the team's input before making decisions. In which situation is the best choice for the charge nurse to make the decisions alone and give direct instructions?
options: Planning the unit's holiday schedule
Choosing a new bedside handoff format
Moving clients during a fire evacuation
Orienting experienced travel nurses to the unit
questions.rationale:
An autocratic leader makes the decisions and directs the activities. It's efficient and focused on the task, which is what an emergency like a fire needs: there's no time for discussion, and everyone must know exactly what to do.

Orienting experienced travel nurses isn't the right answer, even though they're new to the unit. But they're experienced professionals, who do well with explanation and input, not orders. Holiday schedules and a handoff format affect the whole team and aren't urgent, so input builds commitment.

Takeaway: Emergencies and tasks with no time to discuss call for direct, autocratic leadership; otherwise, involve the team.

questions.stem: A nurse manager asks each shift for ideas on reducing falls, leads a discussion of the options, and has the staff choose one together. Which result should the manager plan for?
options: Quick decisions that follow a set protocol
Little need for the manager to coordinate
Close adherence to the existing procedures
More commitment, and a slower decision
questions.rationale:
This is democratic (participative) leadership: the leader encourages discussion and shared decision making, which builds engagement and productivity. Hearing from every shift takes coordination and time, so the decision comes more slowly.

Little need to coordinate isn't the right answer, even though the staff make the choice. But a democratic leader stays involved and coordinates the group; a hands-off leader who doesn't coordinate is laissez-faire. Quick decisions fit an autocratic style, and adherence to procedures a bureaucratic one.

Takeaway: Democratic leadership trades speed for engagement, and needs a leader who coordinates.

questions.stem: Staff on a unit say their manager answers every suggestion with “That's not how the procedure reads,” even when a change would be safe and fit the unit's goals. Which problem is most likely to develop on the unit?
options: Dissatisfaction from the lack of flexibility
Confusion from a lack of clear procedures
Unsafe care from too little supervision of staff
Slow decisions from too many opinions
questions.rationale:
A bureaucratic leader works strictly within the organization's policies and procedures and allows little flexibility, which can leave staff dissatisfied.

Unsafe care from too little supervision isn't the right answer, even though the manager isn't responsive to staff. But this manager supervises closely, by the rules: too little supervision is the risk of a laissez-faire style. Unclear procedures is the opposite of this unit's problem, and slow decisions from many opinions fits a democratic style.

Takeaway: Rules first, little flexibility: bureaucratic leadership, with dissatisfied staff as its risk.

questions.stem: A charge nurse leads two experienced nurses and a new graduate. Midmorning, a client on the unit suddenly deteriorates. Which approach should the charge nurse take with the team today?
options: Let the three nurses organize their own work, as the experienced ones prefer
Direct the team during the emergency, and coach the new graduate closely
Hold a quick team vote before each decision so everyone shares it
Follow the unit's written routine exactly so the new graduate learns it
questions.rationale:
A situational leader adapts the style to the situation and the people: direct leadership while a client is deteriorating, and more guidance for a new graduate than for experienced nurses. Flexibility is the key.

Letting all three organize their own work isn't the right answer: it fits the experienced nurses, but it leaves the new graduate without support and the emergency without direction. A vote is too slow for an emergency, and following the written routine exactly is rigid when the situation has changed.

Takeaway: Match the style to the moment and the person: direct in a crisis, coaching for a novice, hands-off for experts on a routine day.

questions.stem: A charge nurse usually involves the team in decisions. In which situations should the charge nurse give direct instructions instead of asking the team for input?
options: Choosing the theme for the unit's practice council meeting
A client on the unit goes into cardiac arrest
Planning next month's staff education topics
A smoke alarm sounds and the unit must evacuate
A new nurse's client has a falling oxygen saturation
Deciding which shift tries a new break schedule first
questions.rationale:
Direct, autocratic leadership fits emergencies and situations where someone needs clear direction right away: a cardiac arrest, an evacuation, and a new nurse with a client whose oxygen saturation is falling (the novice needs direction, and the client can't wait).

The break schedule isn't the right answer, even though someone has to decide it. But it isn't urgent, and the people affected have useful input, so involving them builds commitment. The council theme and education topics are also good chances for participation.

Takeaway: Urgent and safety-critical, or a novice who needs direction: give direct instructions. Not urgent: involve the team.

questions.stem: A nurse manager's hands-off style worked well with the unit's long-time, skilled staff. After half the staff are replaced by new graduates, missed tasks and near misses increase. Which action should the nurse manager take first?
options: Keep the hands-off style so the new nurses build independence
Ask the staff to vote on how the unit should be led
Give more direction and structure as the new nurses learn
Write a stricter procedure manual and have each nurse sign it
questions.rationale:
A laissez-faire style works only when the group is skilled and committed. The group has changed, and the near misses show it, so the leader adapts (situational leadership): more direction and structure until the new nurses have the skills to work more independently.

A stricter manual isn't the right answer, even though it adds structure. But a rule-based (bureaucratic) fix gives new nurses paperwork, not the direction and coaching they need, and it costs flexibility. Keeping the hands-off style ignores the near misses, and a vote on leadership doesn't help nurses who don't know the work yet.

Takeaway: Hands-off leadership fits experts. When the team changes, the leader's style changes with it.

questions.stem: A nursing student says, “Some people are born leaders, and I'm just not one of them.” Which response by the nurse educator is accurate?
options: “That's often true, since leadership traits are mostly set by adulthood.”
“Leadership comes with a formal title, so you'll learn it once you're promoted.”
“Leaders need a charismatic personality, so focus on your clinical skills.”
“Leadership styles develop through education, training, and experience.”
questions.rationale:
Behavior-based theories hold that leaders develop their style through education, training, and experience, so leadership can be learned.

Leadership traits set by adulthood isn't the right answer: it matches the oldest, trait-based theory (leaders are born with certain traits), which is exactly what the student believes. The class presents behavior-based and later theories, which say leadership is learned. Leadership also doesn't wait for a title, and charisma is one contemporary style, not a requirement.

Takeaway: Trait theory says leaders are born; behavior theory says they're made, through education, training, and experience.

questions.stem: A nurse manager shares a vision of a restraint-free unit, coaches each nurse on alternatives, and asks staff to come up with creative solutions. Staff go well beyond what's required. Which leadership style does the manager's approach fit best?
options: Transformational
Transactional
Charismatic
Laissez-faire
questions.rationale:
A transformational leader motivates the group toward a shared vision, coaches each person (individual consideration), encourages creative problem solving (intellectual stimulation), and often gets performance beyond what's expected.

Charismatic isn't the right answer, even though the manager inspires staff. But a charismatic leader engages the group through personality, while this manager builds the vision, coaches, and asks staff to solve the problem. A transactional leader exchanges rewards for meeting expectations, and a laissez-faire leader steps back.

Takeaway: Vision, coaching, creative problem solving, and results beyond expectations: transformational.

questions.stem: A nurse manager gives staff an extra day off when the unit meets its hand-hygiene audit goal, and corrects nurses when an audit shows a missed step. Which result should the manager expect from this approach?
options: Performance far beyond what's expected
Results that match the expected targets
Little direction, since the manager steps back
Strong loyalty to the manager's personality
questions.rationale:
