This is transactional leadership: rewards in exchange for meeting set goals (contingent reward), and correcting errors when monitoring finds them (management by exception). It tends to produce expected outcomes.

Performance far beyond what's expected isn't the right answer, even though rewards motivate. But going beyond expectations is the mark of transformational leadership, which motivates through a shared vision rather than an exchange. Stepping back is laissez-faire, and loyalty to a personality is charismatic.

Takeaway: Transactional leadership gets the expected results; transformational leadership gets more than expected.

questions.stem: A nurse manager's unit has high staff turnover and burnout, and a rising number of medication errors. Based on the leadership research from class, which approach should the nurse manager work to develop?
options: Passive leadership, giving staff more independence
Transactional leadership, linking rewards to the audit results
Transformational leadership, coaching toward a shared goal
Bureaucratic leadership, tightening the unit's procedures
questions.rationale:
Research on nursing leadership links transformational leadership with better staff well-being, higher job satisfaction, less burnout, and a lower intention to leave, and with client outcomes like fewer medication errors and higher satisfaction. That matches all three of this unit's problems.

Transactional leadership isn't the right answer, even though rewards tied to audits can bring error numbers up to target. But it produces expected outcomes, not the retention and well-being this unit needs. Passive (avoidant) leadership is linked to poorer outcomes, and tighter procedures can add to dissatisfaction.

Takeaway: Turnover, burnout, and safety problems point to transformational leadership, the style the research favors.

questions.stem: On a unit's practice council, nurses, a pharmacist, and a physical therapist each lead the agenda items in their own area, and decisions are made together. Which benefit should the unit expect from this structure?
options: Broader decisions that draw on each member's expertise
Faster decisions, since one leader sets the whole direction
Fewer meetings, since members act independently
Clearer authority, through a single chain of command
questions.rationale:
Shared leadership builds on collective action: leadership moves among members, so decisions draw on more people's expertise, a broader decision-making process.

Clearer authority through one chain of command isn't the right answer, even though a council is a formal structure. But shared leadership spreads leadership across members rather than concentrating it. One leader setting the direction is the opposite of shared leadership, and members who act independently aren't sharing decisions.

Takeaway: Shared leadership spreads leading across the team, for broader decisions built on everyone's expertise.

questions.stem: A nurse manager wants to lower turnover and help staff perform beyond expectations. Which actions should the nurse manager take?
options: Meet with each nurse about goals and offer coaching
Rely mainly on bonuses for meeting audit targets
Share a clear picture of what the unit could become
Step back and let staff handle problems on their own
Invite staff to find creative solutions to unit problems
Act with integrity and keep commitments to staff
questions.rationale:
These are the parts of transformational leadership, the style linked to lower turnover and performance beyond expectations: coaching each nurse (individual consideration), an inspiring vision (inspirational motivation), creative problem solving (intellectual stimulation), and integrity that builds trust (idealized influence).

Bonuses for audit targets isn't the right answer, even though rewards do motivate. But rewards in exchange for meeting targets are transactional, and produce expected results, not results beyond them. Stepping back is a passive, laissez-faire approach, linked to poorer outcomes when the team needs leadership.

Takeaway: Vision, coaching, creativity, and integrity are the four parts of transformational leadership.

questions.stem: Staff at a nursing home say the director of nursing is rarely seen on the units and acts only after a problem becomes serious. Staff turnover is high. Which explanation of this leadership is best supported by the research from class?
options: A hands-off style that works because the staff are experienced
A passive, avoidant style linked to poorer outcomes for staff
A transactional style that corrects errors after they happen
A bureaucratic style focused mainly on the facility's rules
questions.rationale:
Acting only once problems become serious, and being largely absent, is passive-avoidant leadership: passive management by exception and laissez-faire, an absence of leadership. Research found this style far too common in nursing homes, and linked it to poorer leadership outcomes, while transformational leadership is linked to staying on the job.

Transactional correction of errors isn't the right answer, even though the director does react to problems. But a transactional leader monitors actively and corrects errors as they're found; this director waits until problems are serious. A hands-off style that works needs a committed, stable team, and the high turnover says this one isn't working.

Takeaway: Active monitoring and correction is transactional; waiting until problems are serious is passive-avoidant, the style linked to the worst outcomes.

questions.stem: A nurse manager compares the unit's monthly fall rate with the target set in January, and gives staff feedback on the results. Which management function is the manager carrying out?
options: Planning
Organizing
Controlling
Coordinating
questions.rationale:
Controlling uses measures to monitor and evaluate progress toward goals: setting a performance standard, comparing actual results with it, and giving feedback.

Planning isn't the right answer, even though a target was involved. But setting the target in January was planning; comparing this month's results with it is controlling. Organizing assigns staff, equipment, and supplies, and coordinating (directing) motivates people and delegates work.

Takeaway: Set the goal: planning. Measure results against it and give feedback: controlling.

questions.stem: Before flu season, a nurse manager writes a staffing plan to put in place if more than a fifth of the staff call out sick at once. Which kind of plan has the manager written?
options: A strategic plan
An operational plan
A budget plan
A contingency plan
questions.rationale:
A contingency plan prepares for something that may happen, based on how likely it is, like a wave of staff illness during flu season.

A strategic plan isn't the right answer, even though it's also prepared in advance. But a strategic plan sets the organization's long-term outcomes, usually through a committee that gathers data from stakeholders over months. An operational plan carries out day-to-day work, and a budget plans spending.

Takeaway: “If this happens, we'll do that” is a contingency plan; long-term organizational goals are a strategic plan.

questions.stem: The hospital has approved four new beds on a unit. The nurse manager works out which staff, equipment, and supplies will go to the new beds, and who will report to whom. Which management function is the manager carrying out?
options: Organizing
Controlling
Coordinating
Planning
questions.rationale:
Organizing is identifying and assigning resources, from staff to equipment and supplies, and setting out who reports to whom in the structure.

Planning isn't the right answer, even though it all happens before the beds open. But the decision to add the beds was the plan; arranging the people and things to carry it out is organizing. Controlling measures results against standards, and coordinating motivates people and delegates work as it's done.

Takeaway: Deciding the goal and the course of action is planning; lining up the staff, equipment, and structure to do it is organizing.

questions.stem: At the start of a shift, the charge nurse explains the day's goals to the team, delegates tasks to the assistive personnel, and encourages everyone to keep each other updated. Which management function is the charge nurse carrying out?
options: Organizing
Coordinating
Controlling
Planning
questions.rationale:
Coordinating (directing) uses communication to motivate the group and move the work forward, and delegation is part of it.

Organizing isn't the right answer, even though assignments are involved. But organizing identifies and assigns resources; here the charge nurse is communicating, motivating, and handing off tasks as the work begins, which is directing. Controlling measures results, and planning sets the goals.

Takeaway: Communicating, motivating, and delegating while the work goes on is coordinating (directing).

questions.stem: A hospital's leaders want to improve the hospital's nursing outcomes over the next five years. Which step should the leaders take first?
options: Have the chief nursing officer write the plan and announce it
Have each unit manager set its own goals for the year
Form a committee that gathers data from stakeholders
Have the staff vote on the goal at a staff meeting
questions.rationale:
This is a strategic plan: it focuses on the organization's outcomes. Planning starts from assessment data, and a strategic plan usually involves a committee working over several months to gather and analyze data from stakeholders.

Having the chief nursing officer write the plan isn't the right answer, even though leaders are responsible for the strategy. But writing it before gathering data skips the assessment that planning is built on, and leaves out the stakeholders. Unit goals are short-term and fragmented, and a vote chooses a goal without the data to support it.

Takeaway: Planning starts with assessment data; a strategic plan comes from a committee gathering data from stakeholders.

questions.stem: A nurse manager's unit has a goal of cutting central line infections in half this year. Which actions should the nurse manager take to find out whether the unit is meeting the goal?
options: Order more central line dressing kits
Set a monthly infection rate as the standard
Assign a nurse to each line-care task
Compare each month's rate with the standard
Give staff feedback on the results
Draft next year's budget for supplies
questions.rationale:
Finding out whether a goal is being met is controlling: set a performance standard, compare actual results with it, and give feedback.

Ordering more dressing kits isn't the right answer, even though supplies help prevent infections. But that's organizing resources; it doesn't tell the manager whether the goal is being met. Assigning tasks is directing, and next year's budget is planning.

Takeaway: Controlling is a loop: a standard, a comparison with real results, and feedback.

questions.stem: A new nurse asks the preceptor how being accountable differs from being responsible. Which statement by the preceptor matches the definitions from class?
options: “You're responsible to your scope of practice, and accountable for your duties.”
“They mean the same thing in nursing, though managers use them differently.”
“Managers are accountable for outcomes, while staff nurses are responsible for tasks.”
“You're accountable to your scope of practice, and responsible for your duties.”
questions.rationale:
In the class's definitions, a nurse is accountable to something, like the scope of practice, and responsible for carrying out their professional roles and duties.

The first choice isn't the right answer: it uses the same two pieces with the words swapped. Accountable to the standard, responsible for the work. The two terms aren't the same, and both apply to every nurse, not just to managers or just to staff.

Takeaway: Accountable to (the scope of practice); responsible for (your duties).

questions.stem: A charge nurse asks a staff nurse to take the next admission. The staff nurse says, “You're a nurse just like me. You can't tell me what to do.” Which statement about the charge nurse's authority is accurate?
options: The facility gives the charge role the right to direct others' work
Authority comes from seniority, so it depends on years of service
The charge nurse can direct the assistive personnel, but not nurses
Assigning admissions belongs to the nurse manager, not the charge nurse
questions.rationale:
Authority is the right to direct others and their activities to reach outcomes. It comes from the organization: the facility gives the charge role that right, in line with its chain of command.

Authority from seniority isn't the right answer, even though experienced nurses often have influence. But influence and authority are different: authority comes with the position, not the years. A charge nurse directs nurses as well as assistive personnel, and making assignments during the shift is part of the role.

Takeaway: Authority comes from the position the organization gives; influence comes from the person.

questions.stem: Two nurses on a unit have argued about lunch breaks for weeks, and coworkers have started taking sides. Which action should the nurse manager take first?
options: Schedule the two nurses on different shifts for the next month
Meet with both nurses to hear each side and agree on a plan
Write a break policy and post it for the whole unit
Refer both nurses to the employee assistance program
questions.rationale:
Managing conflict is one of a manager's principles, and conflict on a team affects everyone. The first step is to bring the two nurses together, hear each side, and reach an agreement on next steps, which keeps the conflict healthy and resolves it at its source.

Writing a break policy isn't the right answer, even though it addresses the topic. But a policy imposed without talking to the people in conflict leaves the conflict itself unresolved. Separating the nurses avoids it, and the employee assistance program may help later, but it hands off a work problem the manager should address first.

Takeaway: Address conflict directly with the people involved, before rules, reassignments, or referrals.

questions.stem: Halfway through the year, a nurse manager sees that the unit's supply spending is well above the projected budget. Which action should the nurse manager take?
options: Reduce the float staff hours to balance the budget
Ask staff to borrow supplies from other units
Review where costs differ from the projection and adjust
Request a larger budget for next year and keep spending as is
questions.rationale:
Managing resources means knowing how the budget affects care, and adapting when actual expenses differ from the projected ones. So the manager finds out where and why costs differ, and changes practices to match best practice.

Cutting float staff hours isn't the right answer, even though it balances the numbers quickly. But it takes from staffing, which affects safe care, to fix a supply problem it doesn't explain. Borrowing supplies moves the cost elsewhere, and asking for more next year doesn't manage this year's spending.

Takeaway: When actual costs differ from the budget, find the cause and adjust; don't fix one resource by cutting another.

questions.stem: A nurse manager wants to improve staff engagement and the unit's outcome measures. Which actions should the nurse manager take?
options: Involve staff in choosing how to improve a quality measure
Make unit decisions alone so staff can focus on care
Help each team member understand the group's purpose
Address conflicts between staff members early
Wait for staff to ask for help before stepping in
Plan the workday so time goes to the top priorities
questions.rationale:
The principles of management include enhancing performance through staff engagement and participation, building teams whose members understand the group's purpose, managing conflict, and managing time.

Making decisions herself so staff can focus on care isn't the right answer, even though it sounds considerate. But it takes away the participation that builds engagement and improves outcome measures. Waiting for staff to ask for help is passive: problems grow before the manager acts.

Takeaway: Engage staff, build the team around a shared purpose, address conflict early, and manage time.

questions.stem: A hospitalist asks a cardiologist to see a client and advise on managing the client's new atrial fibrillation. The hospitalist stays in charge of the client's care. Which kind of request has the hospitalist made?
options: A transfer of care
A referral
A handoff
A consultation
questions.rationale:
In a consultation, one provider formally asks another for input or advice on how to approach or treat a condition, and keeps managing the client.

A referral isn't the right answer, even though the terms are often used interchangeably. But in a referral, the provider hands responsibility for managing the condition to the other provider. A transfer of care turns all of the client's care over to another provider, and a handoff passes information and responsibility at a shift change or transition.

Takeaway: Consult: advice, and the first provider stays in charge. Referral: the condition's management moves. Transfer: all care moves.

questions.stem: A client's primary care provider sends the client to a wound specialist, who will now manage the client's foot ulcer, while the primary care provider keeps managing the client's other conditions. The client's daughter asks the nurse what happened. Which statement by the nurse is accurate?
options: “Your mother has been referred to the specialist for her ulcer.”
“The specialist is consulting, so your mother's provider decides.”
“Your mother's care has been transferred to the specialist.”
“The specialist will advise, and her provider will treat the ulcer.”
questions.rationale:
In a referral, one provider gives another the responsibility for managing a specific condition: the specialist now manages the ulcer, and the primary care provider keeps the rest.

“Transferred” isn't the right answer, even though the ulcer's care moved. But a transfer of care turns over all of the client's care, and here the primary care provider still manages the other conditions. A consultation (the second and fourth choices) means the specialist only advises, while the first provider keeps managing the condition.

Takeaway: One condition's management moves to another provider: referral. Everything moves: transfer. Advice only: consultation.

questions.stem: A hospital's error reviews keep finding that nurses, pharmacists, and therapists each knew part of a problem, but no one put the pieces together. Which change should the hospital's education council make?
options: Train each discipline separately on its own procedures
Train the disciplines in shared classes and drills
Write more detailed safety policies for each department
Make the provider the single decision maker for care
questions.rationale:
Health professionals educated in silos, only within their own discipline, is one of the things that keeps medical errors going. Training the disciplines together builds the shared understanding and communication that interprofessional teams need.

More detailed department policies isn't the right answer, even though policies feel like a safety fix. But they strengthen the silos instead of connecting them. Separate training is the silo itself, and a single decision maker loses what each discipline brings.

Takeaway: Errors that fall between disciplines call for interprofessional education and teamwork, not more silos.

questions.stem: A hospital is building an interprofessional education program on the Interprofessional Education Collaborative (IPEC) core competency areas. Which areas should the program cover?
options: Roles and responsibilities
Discipline-specific skills checkoffs
Values and ethics for interprofessional practice
Teams and teamwork
Billing for each discipline's services
Interprofessional communication
questions.rationale:
IPEC's core competency has four areas: values and ethics for interprofessional practice, roles and responsibilities, interprofessional communication, and teams and teamwork.

Discipline-specific skills checkoffs isn't the right answer, even though every team member needs skills. But checkoffs within one discipline are silo training, not interprofessional competency. Billing isn't part of the competency.

Takeaway: IPEC's four areas: values and ethics, roles and responsibilities, communication, and teamwork.

questions.stem: A client recovering from a stroke wants to go home and walk to the mailbox. The nurse, physical therapist, occupational therapist, and dietitian each have their own plan, and the plans don't line up. Which action by the nurse best supports collaborative care?
options: Follow the nursing plan and let each discipline follow its own
Ask the provider to decide which discipline's plan comes first
Suggest a team meeting, with the client, to set shared goals
Email the nursing plan to the other disciplines to review
questions.rationale:
Collaborative care is client-centered: the disciplines come together, bring their knowledge and skills, and work toward a common goal with the client, who is always part of the team.

Emailing the nursing plan isn't the right answer, even though it shares information. But it's one-way, and it doesn't make the goals shared. Following separate plans is working in silos, and asking the provider to pick one plan loses the other disciplines' expertise and the client's voice.

Takeaway: Collaboration means one set of goals, built together, with the client at the table.

questions.stem: A provider calls a nurse with a telephone prescription for a new medication for a client. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Repeat it aloud to the provider, then write it in the record later
Ask the provider to text the prescription to the unit's phone
Write it down, and confirm it with the provider at morning rounds
Write it down, read it back as written, and get the provider's OK
questions.rationale:
For a telephone prescription, the nurse records it, reads it back exactly as written to the prescriber, and gets the prescriber's verification (receive, record, read back).

Repeating it aloud isn't the right answer, even though it sounds like a read-back. But the class's rule is to read back what you wrote, not repeat what you heard, since the error can happen in the writing. Confirming at rounds leaves an unverified prescription in the meantime, and a text is not how prescriptions are received.

Takeaway: Record, read back from what you wrote, verify: don't just repeat it.

questions.stem: A nurse calls a provider about a client who had a hip replacement this morning, using SBAR. Which statement should the nurse make for the Assessment part of the call?
options: “I'm concerned she may be bleeding internally.”
“She had a right hip replacement at 8 this morning.”
“I'm calling about Ms. Lane in room 4, who looks pale.”
“I'd like you to see her and order a hemoglobin.”
questions.rationale:
In SBAR, the Assessment is what the nurse thinks the problem is, with the findings that support it: here, a concern about bleeding.

The surgery this morning isn't the right answer, even though it's what makes bleeding likely. But that's Background, the clinical context. “I'm calling about Ms. Lane, who looks pale” is the Situation (what's going on), and asking the provider to come and order a test is the Recommendation or request.

Takeaway: Situation: what's going on. Background: the context. Assessment: what I think the problem is. Recommendation: what I'd like done.

questions.stem: During an I-PASS handoff, the receiving nurse has heard the client's illness severity, summary, and action list, and the situation awareness and contingency plans. Which action should the receiving nurse take next?
options: Thank the nurse and go do the first assessment
Summarize the report back and restate the to-do items
Read the chart to check the information that was given
Ask the charge nurse to confirm the illness severity
questions.rationale:
The last step of I-PASS is Synthesis by the receiver: the receiving nurse summarizes what was heard, asks questions, and restates the key actions and to-do items. It closes the loop, so errors are caught before the giving nurse leaves.

Reading the chart isn't the right answer, even though checking information is good practice. But it doesn't give the giving nurse a chance to correct a misunderstanding, and it comes after the handoff, not in place of its last step. Leaving to assess skips the synthesis, and the illness severity was already given.

Takeaway: A handoff isn't finished until the receiver summarizes it back and asks questions.

questions.stem: During a rapid response, the nurse sees the client's oxygen saturation drop to 84%. The team leader is at the head of the bed giving instructions. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Record the value on the flowsheet for the team leader to see
Tell the nearest team member quietly, so the team isn't distracted
Say the value aloud to the whole team, directed to the leader
Wait until the team leader asks for the latest vital signs
questions.rationale:
A call-out communicates critical information to all team members at once during an emergency, so everyone can anticipate the next steps, and it directs the information to the person responsible for acting on it.

Telling one team member quietly isn't the right answer, even though it seems courteous not to interrupt. But in an emergency, the whole team, and above all the leader, needs the information now. Charting it and waiting to be asked both delay a critical finding.

Takeaway: Critical information in an emergency is called out: aloud, to everyone, directed to the person who acts on it.

questions.stem: A nurse finishes teaching a client how to use a new inhaler at home. Which action should the nurse take to best confirm that the teaching was clear?
options: Ask, “Do you have any questions about the inhaler?”
Ask the client to repeat the steps back word for word
Give the client a printed handout to review at home
Ask the client to explain its use in their own words
questions.rationale:
A teach-back confirms that the nurse explained the information clearly: the client explains what to know or do in their own words.

Repeating the steps word for word isn't the right answer, even though it sounds thorough. But repeating can be done from memory without understanding, while explaining in one's own words shows it. Asking whether the client has questions invites a “no” that confirms nothing, and a handout supports teaching but doesn't check it.

Takeaway: Teach-back: the client explains it in their own words. Check-back: a team member repeats a message to the sender.

questions.stem: A nurse is giving a shift handoff report on a client. Which elements should the nurse include to make the handoff complete?
options: Clear, specific information about the client
A written note in place of a spoken report
Acknowledgment by the receiving nurse
Transfer of responsibility for the client
A brief summary given while heading to another room
Time for the receiving nurse to ask questions
questions.rationale:
A proper handoff transfers responsibility and accountability, gives clear information, is spoken, is acknowledged by the receiver, and leaves time for questions and review.

A written note isn't the right answer, even though writing seems more precise. But handoffs are given verbally, so the receiver can acknowledge and ask questions; a note can support a report, not replace it. A summary given in passing leaves no time for questions, and interruptions during handoffs are a known cause of errors.

Takeaway: A complete handoff is spoken, clear, acknowledged, and open to questions, and it transfers responsibility.

questions.stem: During an emergency, a provider says, “Give furosemide 40 mg IV now.” The nurse replies, “Furosemide 40 mg IV now.” Which response from the provider completes the exchange?
options: “That's correct.”
“Go ahead and give it.”
“Call me with the urine output.”
“Document it as a verbal order.”
questions.rationale:
A check-back is closed-loop communication: the sender gives the message, the receiver repeats it, and the sender confirms that it was heard correctly. The provider's “That's correct” closes the loop.

“Go ahead and give it” isn't the right answer, even though it sounds like approval. But it doesn't confirm that the dose, drug, and route the nurse repeated are right. The other two are reasonable next instructions that also skip the confirmation.

Takeaway: A check-back has three parts: the sender says it, the receiver repeats it, and the sender confirms it.

questions.stem: During this morning's handoff, the day nurse told a new graduate, in front of the client, “I can't believe you didn't get this client's weight.” The new graduate wants to resolve the conflict. Which statement is the best way for the new graduate to start?
options: “You're too hard on new nurses, and it's hurting the whole team.”
“Earlier, you raised the missed weight where the client could hear.”
“I'll get the weight tonight, so let's not bring it up again.”
“Let's ask the charge nurse which shift should do the weights.”
questions.rationale:
The DESC script for conflict starts by Describing the specific situation or behavior with concrete facts. Then the nurse Expresses the concern, Suggests alternatives, and states the Consequences for the client and the team's goals.

Asking the charge nurse isn't the right answer, even though it fixes the workflow question. But it skips talking with the coworker directly and leaves the way the comment was made unresolved. A judgment like “too hard on new nurses” is about the person, not a specific behavior, and promising to drop it avoids the conflict.

Takeaway: DESC: Describe (facts), Express (concern), Suggest (alternatives), Consequences (for the client and team).

questions.stem: Before surgery, a nurse tells the surgeon that the sedated client's consent form lists the left knee, but the surgeon is marking the right knee. The surgeon keeps marking without answering. Which action should the nurse take next?
options: Call the nursing supervisor to the room right away
Note the concern in the client's record and continue the setup
Restate the concern firmly and ask for acknowledgment
Wait for the time-out to bring up the concern again
questions.rationale:
The two-challenge rule: when a first assertive statement is ignored, the nurse is responsible for restating the concern, and the person challenged must acknowledge hearing it. If the concern still isn't resolved, the nurse takes stronger action, involves other team members, and uses the supervisor or the chain of command.

Calling the supervisor right away isn't the right answer: it is part of the rule, but it comes after the second challenge. Waiting for the time-out gives the error more time, and noting the concern and continuing lets a possible wrong-site surgery go ahead.

Takeaway: Challenge twice; if the concern is still ignored, go up the chain of command. Anyone can stop the line for safety.

questions.stem: A nurse thinks a client with a new oxygen requirement isn't safe to discharge today. The nurse has told the provider, “I'm concerned about this discharge,” and then, “I'm uncomfortable with it,” and both statements were brushed aside. Which statement should the nurse make next?
options: “I'm a little worried about the discharge plan.”
“Could we think again about the discharge plan?”
“I'm uncomfortable with it, but it's your decision to make.”
“This is a safety issue. I can't support the discharge.”
questions.rationale:
CUS gives assertive statements in rising order: “I'm Concerned,” “I'm Uncomfortable,” and “This is a Safety issue.” This nurse has already used the first two, and both were brushed aside, so the next step is naming the safety issue, which signals that the plan should stop.

“I'm uncomfortable” isn't the right answer: it sounds firm, but the nurse has already said it, and ending with “it's your decision” takes the challenge back. The first two choices drop back to a level of concern that was already dismissed.

Takeaway: CUS climbs from Concerned to Uncomfortable to Safety issue; “safety issue” means stop and address it.

questions.stem: A charge nurse wants the team to talk about what went well and what to change after a rapid response on the unit. When is the best time for this session?
options: Soon after the event, in a short, structured talk
At the start of the next shift, during the brief
During the event, as soon as the client is stable
At the next monthly staff meeting, with the manager
questions.rationale:
A debrief is a short, structured, informal exchange soon after an event, to improve the team's performance through lessons learned and to reinforce what went well.

The next shift's brief isn't the right answer, even though it's a team meeting. But a brief shares the plan before work starts, and many of the people involved won't be there. During the event is the time for a huddle, to adjust the plan, and a monthly meeting is too late for details to be fresh.

Takeaway: Brief before (share the plan), huddle during (adjust it), debrief after (learn from it).

questions.stem: A charge nurse sees a new nurse skip the two-identifier check while giving a client's medication. Which features should the charge nurse's feedback have?
options: Given soon after the missed check
Focused on the behavior, not the nurse's character
Saved for the new nurse's annual evaluation
Specific about the step that was missed
Linked to how the missed step could affect the client
Noting what the new nurse did well
Given in front of the team as a teaching moment
questions.rationale:
Formative feedback improves team performance. It's timely (soon after the behavior), respectful (about behaviors, not personal attributes), specific, directed toward improvement, appreciative (it notes what the nurse does well), considerate, and client focused (how the behavior affects the client).

Giving it in front of the team isn't the right answer, even though others could learn too. But feedback is considerate: correction in front of coworkers isn't, and it makes the nurse defensive. Saving it for the annual evaluation loses the timeliness that makes feedback work.

Takeaway: Good feedback is timely, specific, respectful, appreciative, considerate, and client focused.

questions.stem: A nurse notices that a coworker, on her third double shift this week, has twice nearly hung the wrong IV bag this shift. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Report the near misses to the nurse manager after the shift
Point out the near misses and offer to double-check her IVs
Fill out an incident report on both near misses before leaving
Suggest that the coworker ask for fewer double shifts next week
questions.rationale:
Cross-monitoring and mutual support mean watching each other's back: noticing a teammate's fatigue and workload (the I'M SAFE checklist), and offering help right away, so mistakes are caught before they reach a client.

The incident report isn't the right answer: near misses should be reported, but reporting can wait until the client is safe, and it doesn't protect this shift's clients. Telling the manager after the shift also leaves the rest of the shift unprotected, and fewer shifts next week doesn't help today.

Takeaway: When a teammate is at risk of error, back them up now; report and fix the system after the clients are safe.

questions.stem: Before surgery, a nurse has twice told the surgeon that the sedated client's consent form lists the left knee, but the surgeon marked the other knee, didn't respond either time, and is calling for the time-out. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Stop the line, and call the charge nurse or supervisor now
Restate the concern a third time and wait for an answer
Note both concerns in the record, and assist as directed
Ask the anesthesia provider to raise it with the surgeon after the case
questions.rationale:
The two-challenge rule: the nurse has voiced the concern twice and it's still ignored, so it's time for stronger action. Anyone can stop the line for a safety breach, and the nurse brings in the chain of command, the charge nurse or supervisor, before the procedure goes on.

Restating it a third time isn't the right answer: restating was the right move after the first challenge, but after two challenges the rule calls for escalation. Noting it and assisting lets a possible wrong-site surgery go ahead, and raising it after the case is too late.

Takeaway: Challenge twice; if the concern is still ignored, stop the line and go up the chain of command.

questions.stem: A nurse has told the provider, “I'm concerned,” then “I'm uncomfortable,” and finally “This is a safety issue,” about discharging a client with a new oxygen requirement. The provider writes the discharge order anyway. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Prepare the discharge, since the provider has written the order
Ask the client whether they feel ready to go home today
Document the disagreement, and give the discharge teaching
Take the concern up the chain of command before the client leaves
questions.rationale:
The nurse has used all three CUS statements, ending with “This is a safety issue,” and the provider is going ahead anyway. The next step is the chain of command, the charge nurse and then the nursing supervisor, before the client leaves, since an unsafe discharge can't be undone afterward.

Asking the client isn't the right answer: it sounds like assessing first, but how the client feels doesn't settle a safety concern about oxygen needs. Preparing the discharge and documenting while teaching both let the unsafe plan go ahead.

Takeaway: When “This is a safety issue” is still ignored, use the chain of command before the harm happens.

questions.stem: A nurse used DESC to talk privately with a coworker who keeps leaving tasks undone at handoff. Two weeks later nothing has changed, and today a client missed a scheduled dose because of it. Which action should the nurse take now?
options: Use DESC with the coworker again at the next handoff
Finish the coworker's tasks at each handoff from now on
Bring the pattern to the nurse manager, with dates and facts
Ask the other nurses to raise it with the coworker too
questions.rationale:
The nurse started the right way, with a private, direct conversation using DESC. It didn't work, and now the pattern has affected a client's care, so it goes to the nurse manager, whose role includes managing conflict and staff performance. Bringing dates and facts keeps it about the behavior, not the person. (The missed dose is also reported through the facility's incident reporting.)

Using DESC again isn't the right answer: it's the right tool for a first conversation, but repeating it after a client was affected leaves clients at risk. Finishing the coworker's tasks hides the problem, and asking other nurses to step in turns a work problem into a group conflict.

Takeaway: Try a direct, private conversation first; when it doesn't work, or a client is affected, go up the chain of command with the facts.

questions.stem: Which action should the charge nurse take first?
options: Assess the client in room 12 personally before anyone calls the surgeon
Meet privately with the senior nurse about her comments to the new RN
Tell the new RN to call the surgeon now, since the client has to come first
Go with the new RN to call the surgeon now, using SBAR to report on room 12
questions.rationale:
The client in room 12 shows signs of bleeding and early shock: a rising heart rate, a falling blood pressure, low urine output, and drainage past the outline. The surgeon must hear now. The new RN's fear of the surgeon is what's stopping the call, so the charge nurse goes with her and makes the call with SBAR: the client gets care, and the new RN is coached.

Assessing the client personally isn't the right answer: assessing before acting is often right, but the new RN's findings are recent and clear, and another assessment only delays the call. Telling the new RN to call doesn't remove what has stopped her so far. Meeting with the senior nurse is needed, but after the client is safe.

Takeaway: The client's safety comes before the team's problems. When fear blocks a call, the leader removes the barrier by making the call with the nurse.

questions.stem: Which actions should the charge nurse take about the senior nurse's behavior toward the new RN?
options: Bring up the behavior at the next staff huddle, so the whole team hears it addressed
Meet with the senior nurse privately and soon, and describe the specific behaviors
Move the new RN to another unit, so she doesn't have to work with the senior nurse
Follow the unit's code of conduct, and tell the nurse manager about the pattern
Write down what the new RN reported, with the dates and the words that were used
Wait to act until the charge nurse sees the behavior personally
questions.rationale:
Belittling a new nurse in front of a client, and refusing to help, is bullying, which harms teamwork and client safety. The charge nurse addresses it privately and soon, naming the specific behaviors; writes down what was reported, with dates and words; and follows the unit's code of conduct, bringing in the manager, since it's a pattern.

Waiting to see it personally isn't the right answer: it seems fair to the senior nurse, but a reported pattern of bullying needs action now, and the private meeting gives the senior nurse a chance to respond. Raising it at a huddle shames her in public, and moving the new RN punishes the person who was bullied.

Takeaway: Address bullying privately, promptly, and specifically; document it; and follow the policy. Don't make the target move.

questions.stem: A hospital is starting TeamSTEPPS training on every unit. A staff nurse asks what the program is meant to do. Which response by the nurse educator is accurate?
options: “It sets the staffing ratios each unit has to follow.”
“It gives managers a tool to rate each nurse's work.”
“It teaches team skills that make care safer for clients.”
“It replaces SBAR with one new handoff format.”
questions.rationale:
TeamSTEPPS (Team Strategies and Tools to Enhance Performance and Patient Safety) is an evidence-based framework for teamwork across health care. It teaches four skills (communication, team leadership, situation monitoring, and mutual support) so teams give safe, reliable care and build a lasting culture of safety.

A tool to rate each nurse's work isn't the right answer: the program includes a team performance observation tool, but that tool looks at how a team works together, not at one nurse's evaluation. TeamSTEPPS doesn't set staffing ratios, and it doesn't replace SBAR: SBAR is one of its communication tools.

Takeaway: TeamSTEPPS is an evidence-based teamwork program for client safety, built on communication, team leadership, situation monitoring, and mutual support.

questions.stem: During a busy shift, a nurse notices that a coworker is staying with a client in respiratory distress while three of her other clients' call lights are on. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Offer to see her other clients while she stays with this one
Tell the charge nurse that the coworker has fallen behind with her clients
Remind the coworker to call for help sooner the next time she's this busy
Ask the coworker what she needs once the client in distress is stable
questions.rationale:
Mutual support, one of the TeamSTEPPS skills, means anticipating and meeting teammates' needs through awareness of their workload. The nurse sees the overload and steps in with specific help now, so the coworker can stay with the unstable client and the other clients are seen.

Telling the charge nurse isn't the right answer: the charge nurse manages the workload, but it reports a problem the nurse can help with right away, and it frames the coworker as falling behind. Asking once the client is stable waits while call lights go unanswered, and advice for next time doesn't help anyone now.

Takeaway: When a teammate is overloaded, offer specific help now; mutual support is part of keeping every client safe.

questions.stem: A client in a small rural hospital needs heart surgery that the hospital doesn't offer. The surgical team at a regional heart center will take over all of the client's care there. Which statement by the nurse to the client is accurate?
options: “The surgeon will advise your doctor here, who stays in charge of your care.”
“Your doctor here will manage your care except for your heart problem.”
“The surgeon will see you by video while you stay here for your care.”
“Your care will be turned over to the surgeons where you're going.”
questions.rationale:
This is a transfer of care: care is systematically turned over to another provider, here the surgical team at the heart center. The client's care moves with the client.

The doctor here managing all but the heart problem isn't the right answer: that's a referral, where one provider hands over management of one condition while keeping the rest. The surgeon advising the doctor here, or seeing the client by video while the local team stays in charge, describes a consultation: advice only.

Takeaway: Consult = advice, and the first provider keeps the client. Refer = another provider manages one condition. Transfer = care is turned over to another provider.

questions.stem: On a medical unit, a council of staff nurses reviewed the evidence and voted to change how bedside shift report is done. A new nurse asks why staff nurses, not the manager, made the decision. Which response by the charge nurse is accurate?
options: “Our manager is a laissez-faire leader who leaves decisions to the staff.”
“Our hospital uses shared governance, so staff help decide on practice.”
“Our manager is a bureaucratic leader, so policy changes go through staff.”
“Our unit uses team nursing, so the team leaders decide on practice.”
questions.rationale:
In shared governance, staff nurses share decision-making with management about their own practice, quality, and education, usually through councils. A staff council reviewing evidence and deciding on the shift report process is shared governance at work. It's a structure of the organization, not one leader's personal style.

Laissez-faire isn't the right answer: staff are making the decision, but laissez-faire is a hands-off leader's style, while shared governance is a formal structure in which staff hold real responsibility, with the manager still involved. A bureaucratic leader holds to rules and procedures with little flexibility, and team nursing is a way of assigning care, not of deciding practice.

Takeaway: Shared governance is a formal structure where nurses share decisions about their practice; don't confuse it with a hands-off leader.

questions.stem: After interprofessional rounds, a new nurse who stayed silent while the team planned a client's discharge says, “With all the specialists there, I didn't think my input was needed.” Which guidance should the charge nurse give?
options: Suggest reading the other disciplines' notes before the next rounds
Suggest sharing any concerns with the charge nurse after rounds end
Point out that the provider makes the final call on the discharge plan
Point out what the nurse knows about the client that the others don't
questions.rationale:
The IPEC core competencies include roles and responsibilities: each member knows their own role and the others', and brings it to the team. The nurse spends the most time with the client and knows things the specialists may not (how the client manages self-care, who is at home, what the client understands). Showing the new nurse what nursing adds prepares them to speak up.

Sharing concerns with the charge nurse after rounds isn't the right answer: it feels safe for a new nurse, but it keeps the nurse's knowledge out of the team's plan. Reading the other disciplines' notes helps a nurse understand their roles, but not the nurse's own. Pointing out that the provider decides reinforces the idea that the nurse's voice doesn't matter.

Takeaway: On an interprofessional team, every member brings their own role's knowledge to the plan, and the nurse's view of the whole client is part of it.

questions.stem: A charge nurse makes every decision about the team's assignments and breaks, telling the staff, “I know what's best for you, and I'll look after you.” Staff feel cared for but have no say. Which leadership style is this?
options: Laissez-faire
Transformational
Situational
Paternalistic
questions.rationale:
A paternalistic leader is a caring form of the autocratic leader: decisions stay with the leader, “for the good” of the staff, who are looked after but not involved.

Transformational isn't the right answer: the leader cares about the staff, but a transformational leader involves and inspires the staff and shares a vision; this leader keeps every decision.

Takeaway: Paternalistic = autocratic decisions with a caring tone.

questions.stem: A nurse is planning teaching for a client who has a new colostomy. Which learning objective belongs in the psychomotor domain?
options: The client will describe the signs of a blocked stoma by day 3.
The client will empty and rinse the pouch without help by day 3.
The client will share feelings about the change in body image by day 3.
The client will list foods that commonly cause gas by day 3.
questions.rationale:
The psychomotor domain is the "skill" domain: doing something with the hands and body. Emptying and rinsing the pouch is a skill the nurse can watch the client perform.

Describing the signs of a blocked stoma isn't the right answer. It's about the stoma and sounds practical, but describing is thinking: the cognitive domain. Listing foods is cognitive too. Sharing feelings about body image belongs to the affective ("feeling") domain.

Takeaway: Cognitive is thinking (describe, list, explain), affective is feeling (accept, value, share feelings), and psychomotor is doing (a skill you can watch).

questions.stem: A nurse has finished teaching a client how to use a metered-dose inhaler with a spacer. Which method should the nurse use to evaluate this learning?
options: Ask the client to explain each step of using the inhaler
Give the client a short written quiz on the spacer steps
Ask how confident she feels with the inhaler and spacer
Watch the client use the inhaler and spacer
questions.rationale:
Using an inhaler with a spacer is a psychomotor skill, so the best evidence of learning is a return demonstration: the nurse watches the client do it and corrects the technique.

Explaining each step isn't the right answer: teach-back is so common, but a client can recite the steps and still hold the inhaler wrong or breathe in too fast. Teach-back checks understanding (cognitive); a skill needs to be seen. A written quiz also checks only knowledge, and how confident she feels is self-report, which can't show whether the technique is correct.

Takeaway: Match the evaluation to the domain: a skill is evaluated by watching it (return demonstration); knowledge by teach-back, questions, or a test.

questions.stem: A client newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes correctly explains his meal plan and names the carbohydrate foods in it. He then says, “I'm not going to be one of those people who can't have cake at a party. Diets are for sick people.” Which action should the nurse take next?
options: Explore what this diagnosis means to the client
Review the meal plan again with a new handout
Have the client plan a full day of meals on paper
Document that the teaching outcome was met
questions.rationale:
The client has shown cognitive learning (he can explain the plan), but his statement shows he hasn't accepted the diagnosis or valued the change: affective learning hasn't happened. The nurse addresses it by exploring what the diagnosis means to him, his feelings and beliefs, before expecting the behavior to change.

Documenting that the outcome was met isn't the right answer, even though he passed the knowledge check. But confirmed cognitive learning doesn't ensure affective learning, and he has just said he won't follow the plan. Reviewing the plan again and planning a day of meals both repeat cognitive teaching he has already mastered.

Takeaway: Knowing isn't accepting. When a client can explain the plan but rejects it, teach to the affective domain: explore feelings, beliefs, and values.

questions.stem: A nurse is writing affective-domain objectives for a client recovering from a myocardial infarction. Which objectives should the nurse include?
options: The client expresses feelings about returning to work.
The client states that quitting smoking is worth the effort.
The client takes his own radial pulse for one full minute.
The client lists three warning signs of a heart attack.
The client chooses to join a cardiac rehabilitation support group.
The client explains how nitroglycerin relieves chest pain.
questions.rationale:
The affective domain covers feelings, attitudes, and values. Expressing feelings about returning to work, stating that quitting is worth it (valuing a change), and choosing to join a support group (acting on a value) are all affective.

Explaining how nitroglycerin works isn't the right answer: it's about the client's own treatment and sounds personal, but explaining is cognitive, as is listing warning signs. Taking a radial pulse is a skill: psychomotor.

Takeaway: Look at the verb: express, value, choose, and accept are affective; list and explain are cognitive; perform and demonstrate are psychomotor.

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching the parent of an infant how to give a liquid medication with an oral syringe. Which teaching strategy should the nurse use?
options: Give a printed sheet with a picture of each step
Discuss each step with the parent, then answer any questions
Demonstrate it, then have the parent practice giving a dose
Show a short video on giving oral medications
questions.rationale:
Measuring and giving a dose with a syringe is a psychomotor skill, and psychomotor skills need practice: discussion alone isn't enough. The nurse demonstrates, then has the parent practice, correcting as needed.

Discussing the steps and answering questions isn't the right answer: it's interactive and invites questions, but the parent never handles the syringe. A picture sheet and a video are useful supports that use the eyes, but neither gives practice.

Takeaway: Skills are learned by doing: demonstrate, then have the learner practice until performance is correct.

questions.stem: A nurse's teaching plan for a client starting warfarin has three objectives: the client will explain why to keep vitamin K intake steady, will brush with a soft toothbrush, and will accept the need for regular blood tests. Which evaluation method matches the first objective?
options: Watch the client brush his teeth with the soft toothbrush
Ask the client how he feels about regular blood tests
Have him tell, in his own words, why leafy greens matter
Check the client's INR result at the next clinic visit
questions.rationale:
The first objective is cognitive: the client will explain a reason. The matching evaluation is to ask him to explain it in his own words.

Checking the INR isn't the right answer, even though it's objective data and a stable INR is the goal of the teaching. But many things change an INR, and a lab result doesn't show whether the client understands vitamin K. Watching him brush evaluates the second (psychomotor) objective, and asking how he feels about blood tests evaluates the third (affective) one.

Takeaway: Each objective's verb names its evaluation: explain is checked by asking, perform by watching, and accept by listening for feelings and values.

questions.stem: A nurse taught a client with a new ileostomy how to care for it. Which observations should the nurse document as evidence that learning occurred?
options: Changes the pouch correctly while the nurse watches
Describes, in his own words, when to call the provider
Nods and says “that makes sense” after each step
Signs the form stating that teaching was received
Watched the full ostomy care video in his room
Empties the pouch on his own when it is one-third full
questions.rationale:
Evidence of learning is a change in behavior that can be observed and measured. Changing the pouch correctly (return demonstration), describing when to call in his own words (teach-back), and emptying the pouch on his own at the right time are all behaviors the nurse can see.

Nodding and saying "that makes sense" isn't the right answer. It sounds like understanding, but agreement isn't evidence: clients often nod to be polite. Signing a form shows teaching was given, not learned, and watching a video is exposure to information, not proof of learning.

Takeaway: Document what the client did or said in his own words, not that he agreed, signed, or watched.

questions.stem: A client recovering from a stroke must learn to walk with a quad cane before discharge. Which outcome statement should the nurse write for this teaching?
options: Walks 50 feet with the quad cane, using the correct sequence, by discharge
Understands how to use the quad cane safely and correctly by discharge
Watches the physical therapist walk with the quad cane by discharge
Feels confident about walking with the quad cane at home by discharge
questions.rationale:
A learning outcome names a behavior the learner will perform that can be observed and measured, with a time frame. Walking 50 feet with the correct sequence can be watched and checked, and it fits the skill being taught.

Understands how to use the cane isn't the right answer: understanding sounds like learning, but "understands" can't be observed or measured. Watching the therapist describes something the client sees, not something the client does. Feeling confident is affective and matters, but it doesn't show the skill was learned.

Takeaway: Write outcomes with an action verb you can observe (walks, demonstrates, states), a measure, and a time frame; avoid "understands" and "knows".

questions.stem: A nurse has taught a client with newly diagnosed hypertension about a low-sodium diet. Which statement by the client shows learning in the affective domain?
options: “I should keep my sodium under the limit I was given.”
“I can find the sodium on a food label in the store.”
“High sodium makes my body hold on to extra fluid.”
“I've decided my health is worth cutting back on salt.”
questions.rationale:
Affective learning is a change in attitudes and values. Saying that her health is worth cutting back on salt shows she values the change.

Keeping sodium under the limit isn't the right answer. It sounds committed, but it restates a rule she was taught: cognitive. Explaining that sodium holds fluid is also cognitive. Finding sodium on a label is a skill she can show in the store.

Takeaway: Affective statements reveal what the client values or has decided ("worth it", "I've decided"); cognitive statements repeat facts or rules.

questions.stem: A nurse plans to teach a client, 1 day after a hip replacement, how to use a walker. The client is grimacing, rates pain 8 on a scale of 0 to 10, and asks, “Can we do this later?” Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Begin teaching, keeping the session short and simple
Give the prescribed pain medication, then return to teach
Leave a handout on walker safety for the client to read
Ask the physical therapist to teach the walker instead
questions.rationale:
Pain is a physiologic factor that blocks learning, and physical needs come before teaching (Maslow). The nurse treats the pain first, then teaches when the client can focus and move.

A short, simple session isn't the right answer: keeping it brief sounds considerate, but a client in severe pain can't learn a new skill, however short the lesson. A handout doesn't relieve the pain and can't teach a skill that needs practice. The physical therapist would face the same pain.

Takeaway: Pain, fatigue, and strong emotions block learning. Meet the physical need first, then teach.

questions.stem: A nurse is assessing whether a client with newly diagnosed diabetes is ready to learn about insulin. Which findings suggest readiness?
options: Asks how the insulin will fit with her work schedule
Changes the subject whenever the diagnosis comes up
Picks up the insulin pen on the tray and asks to hold it
Keeps the television on while the nurse is explaining
Has canceled two diabetes education appointments
Says she wants to be able to take care of herself at home
questions.rationale:
A client who is ready to learn asks questions (how insulin fits her work), shows interest (asks to hold the pen), and recognizes the learning need (wants to care for herself).

Keeping the television on may look harmless, but it shows inattention, a cue that she isn't ready. Changing the subject suggests she hasn't accepted the diagnosis, and canceling appointments is a classic sign of low motivation.

Takeaway: Ready learners ask questions, reach for the equipment, and name their own goals; minimal interest, inattention, and canceled appointments signal low readiness.

questions.stem: A client learned of a cancer diagnosis an hour ago and is crying. The nurse has wound care teaching scheduled before the client's discharge this afternoon. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Sit with the client and encourage her to talk about the news
Teach the wound care now, since discharge is set for today
Give the written wound care instructions and offer to answer questions
Teach the wound care to the client's husband while she rests
questions.rationale:
Strong emotions such as fear, grief, and anxiety inhibit learning. The client can't take in wound care right now, so the nurse first responds to her emotional state, then teaches when she's able to focus.

Teaching her husband isn't the right answer, even though involving a support person is often wise, and he can help at home. But it bypasses the client, who is the learner, and leaves her distress unaddressed. Teaching now ignores the emotional barrier, and written instructions handed to a crying client won't be read or understood.

Takeaway: Address strong emotions before teaching; learning can't happen until the client can focus.

questions.stem: A client tells the nurse, “I never finished school, and I don't read much.” Which teaching material should the nurse choose for this client?
options: A detailed handout written at a high school level
A large-print booklet with each medical term defined
A short video with pictures that shows each step
A website the client can read at home later
questions.rationale:
Clients with minimal literacy need information presented through audio or visuals. A short video with pictures teaches without depending on reading.

A large-print booklet with terms defined isn't the right answer: it seems to make reading easier, but large print helps vision, not reading ability, and definitions add more words. A high school-level handout and a website both depend on reading.

Takeaway: For low literacy, use pictures, audio, video, demonstration, and plain spoken language; don't just make the print bigger.

questions.stem: Over three visits, a client says he forgot his reading glasses each time the nurse hands him printed material, and he asks his wife to fill out his forms. He follows spoken directions well. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Give the client large-print handouts at the next visit
Assess the client's literacy in a private, respectful way
Teach the wife, since she manages the paperwork at home
Refer the client to an eye care provider for a vision exam
questions.rationale:
Repeated excuses ("forgot my glasses"), asking others to complete forms, and doing well with spoken directions are common cues of low literacy. The nurse assesses reading ability privately and respectfully, so the teaching plan can fit the client without shaming him.

A vision exam isn't the right answer: the client blames his glasses, but he follows spoken directions well and the pattern points to reading, not seeing. Large print rests on the same wrong assumption. Teaching the wife leaves out the client, who is the learner.

Takeaway: Excuses to avoid reading and relying on others for forms suggest low literacy: assess it privately, then teach with spoken words, pictures, and demonstration.

questions.stem: A nurse is planning when and where to teach a client how to change a dressing. Which choice best supports learning?
options: Right after the client's physical therapy session
At the bedside while the roommate has visitors
Just before discharge, so the steps are fresh
After the client's nap, in a quiet room
questions.rationale:
Timing and environment are factors that help learning. After a nap, in a quiet room, the client is rested and free of distractions.

Just before discharge isn't the right answer: the steps would be fresh, but last-minute teaching leaves no time for practice, questions, or reteaching. Right after physical therapy the client is likely tired, and a roommate's visitors distract.

Takeaway: Teach when the client is rested and comfortable, in a quiet place, with enough time to practice before discharge.

questions.stem: A client with type 2 diabetes shows little interest in teaching about diet, but lights up when he talks about playing soccer with his grandchildren. Which approach is most likely to motivate the client?
options: Explain the long-term complications of uncontrolled diabetes
Give him a detailed meal plan with exact portions to follow
Tell him the provider expects his A1C to improve by next visit
Link the diet changes to staying active with his family
questions.rationale:
One of the best ways to raise motivation is to relate the learning to something the client values. Connecting the diet to staying active with his family, like playing soccer with his grandchildren, gives him a reason that matters to him.

Explaining long-term complications isn't the right answer: the facts are true and serious, but fear of distant problems rarely motivates someone who isn't engaged. A detailed meal plan adds content before he's interested, and the provider's expectation is someone else's goal, not his.

Takeaway: Motivation grows when teaching connects to what the client values; find it, then build the teaching around it.

questions.stem: A client with hypertension hasn't been taking her prescribed medication, and a coworker calls her “noncompliant.” Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Reteach the purpose of the medication and its schedule
Ask what makes the daily doses hard for her
Document the client's nonadherence in the medical record
Ask the provider about switching to a once-daily medication
questions.rationale:
Before labeling a client noncompliant, the nurse finds out why she isn't following the plan: cost, side effects, confusion, beliefs, or access. Asking what has made it hard is the assessment that guides everything else.

Reteaching isn't the right answer: a learning need seems likely, but it assumes the reason is lack of knowledge, and she may understand perfectly and be unable to afford the drug. Switching medications is a solution before the problem is known, and documenting nonadherence applies the label the nurse should hold off on.

Takeaway: Don't label a client noncompliant until you know why; assess the reason first, then plan teaching or other help.

questions.stem: A nurse is asked to teach a client how to use a newly prescribed insulin pen. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Write learning objectives for the insulin pen session
Choose a video that shows how to use the insulin pen
Find out what the client already knows about insulin
Demonstrate the pen using a practice injection pad
questions.rationale:
Teaching follows the nursing process, and the first step is assessment: what the client already knows, whether he can learn, his readiness, and how he prefers to learn. Every later step depends on it.

Writing objectives isn't the right answer: planning comes early, but objectives can't be set before the nurse knows what the client needs. Choosing a video and demonstrating are implementation steps that come later.

Takeaway: The first step in teaching is assessing the learner: background knowledge, ability, readiness, and preferences.

questions.stem: A client with newly diagnosed heart failure has several learning needs before discharge. Which approach should the nurse use to set the order of teaching?
options: Decide on the priorities together with the client
Start with the topic the provider listed first in the orders
Follow the order of topics on the unit's standard care plan
Start with the topic the nurse considers the most complex
questions.rationale:
Teaching priorities are best set by the nurse and the client together. When the client's own priorities are addressed, the client is more motivated to keep going with the remaining learning needs.

Following the standard care plan isn't the right answer: it's organized and evidence-based, but it isn't tailored to this client and leaves the client out of the decision. The provider's order and the nurse's sense of complexity also skip the client's participation.

Takeaway: Involve the client in every step of planning, including the order of topics; it raises motivation.

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching a client with heart failure about self-care at home. Which statement by the nurse uses language best suited to client teaching?
options: “Monitor for edema and report any dyspnea on exertion to your provider.”
“Weigh yourself each morning after you use the bathroom, before you eat.”
“Restrict fluids to 1,500 mL per day, and keep a record of your I&O.”
“Watch for signs of fluid volume excess, such as rapid weight gain.”
questions.rationale:
When teaching, the nurse communicates clearly and concisely, in a layperson's vocabulary. "Weigh yourself each morning after you use the bathroom, before you eat" uses everyday words and tells the client exactly what to do.

"Watch for signs of fluid volume excess" isn't the right answer: it gives an example the client can recognize, but "fluid volume excess" is nursing language. Edema and dyspnea on exertion are medical terms, and mL and I&O are abbreviations a client may not know.

Takeaway: Teach in plain words the client uses every day, and say exactly what to do; translate medical terms and abbreviations.

questions.stem: A client with newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes drinks six cans of regular soda a day. The nurse and the client are setting a goal. Which goal is best?
options: The client will stop drinking regular soda starting today.
The client will understand how soda raises blood glucose.
The client will drink less regular soda over the next few months.
The client will swap three daily sodas for water within 2 weeks.
questions.rationale:
The behavior change expected from teaching must be realistic, and a goal must be measurable and time-bound. Replacing three sodas with water within 2 weeks is a specific, achievable first step.

Stopping all soda today isn't the right answer: it's the healthiest goal, but quitting a six-a-day habit at once is unrealistic and sets the client up to fail. Understanding how soda raises glucose can't be measured, and drinking less over the next months has no amount and no clear deadline.

Takeaway: Good goals are realistic, measurable, and time-bound; a reachable first step beats an ideal the client can't meet.

questions.stem: A nurse is planning how to teach a client to care for a new tracheostomy at home. Which plan best supports learning?
options: Start with cleaning the outer area, then add steps over several sessions
Cover the whole procedure in one session so the client sees the full process
Teach the hardest step first, while the client is most alert and rested
Give the full procedure in writing, and review it on the day of discharge
questions.rationale:
Learning is helped when information moves from simple to complex and key points are repeated. Starting with a simple part and adding steps over several sessions builds the skill and gives practice each time.

Teaching the hardest step first isn't the right answer: the client's alertness matters, but starting with the hardest part breaks the simple-to-complex rule and can discourage the client. Every step in one session overloads the learner, and written steps reviewed on discharge day leave no time to practice.

Takeaway: Build from simple to complex, spread a skill over several sessions, and repeat key steps.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the unit's handout on inhaler use before teaching a 70-year-old client whose primary language is Spanish. Which findings mean the handout shouldn't be used as it is?
options: It is printed only in English.
It shows an inhaler model the unit no longer stocks.
It uses large print and simple drawings.
It was last updated eleven years ago.
It covers the steps in the client's plan of care.
It was written by the respiratory therapy department.
questions.rationale:
Teaching content must be accurate, current, consistent with the care the client gets, and adjusted for the learner's age, culture, and ability. A handout only in English isn't adjusted for this client, one showing an inhaler she won't use isn't consistent, and one eleven years old may not be current.

Written by respiratory therapy isn't a problem: it wasn't written by nursing, but a reliable, expert source is a strength. Large print and simple drawings suit an older adult, and covering the plan-of-care steps means it matches the learning outcomes.

Takeaway: Before using teaching material, check that it's accurate, current, consistent with the client's care, and fitted to the client's age, language, and abilities.

questions.stem: A nurse is preparing a teaching plan for a client who has a new ileostomy. Which action is most likely to increase the client's motivation to follow the plan?
options: Give the client a copy of the finished plan to keep
Ask the wound care nurse to explain the plan to the client
Involve the client in each step of making the plan
Show the client the plan the unit uses for ostomy clients
questions.rationale:
A teaching plan is best made with the client's participation, which raises the client's motivation. Involving the client in each step makes it the client's plan, not the nurse's.

Asking the wound care nurse to explain it isn't the right answer: a specialist adds expertise, but explaining a finished plan still leaves the client out of making it. A copy to keep and the unit's standard plan are handed to the client rather than built with the client.

Takeaway: Clients follow plans they helped make: involve the client in setting goals, priorities, and methods.

questions.stem: A nurse is planning to teach a client how to check her own blood glucose. Which plan best follows the principles of effective teaching?
options: Explain the steps clearly, and give her a written list of them
Have her watch a video, then answer her questions about it
Show the steps, have her practice, and give her a picture guide
Explain the steps twice, then ask if she has any questions
questions.rationale:
Teaching that uses more than one sense enhances learning, and psychomotor skills need practice. Showing, practicing, and a picture guide combine seeing, doing, and a reminder for home.

Explaining the steps twice isn't the right answer: repetition does reinforce learning, but it's still only hearing, with no practice of the skill. A written list and a video with questions add a sense but still skip hands-on practice.

Takeaway: Combine senses (see, hear, do), and always include practice when teaching a skill.

questions.stem: A nurse has explained a new medication schedule to a client. Which statement by the nurse best confirms the client's understanding?
options: “To be sure I was clear, tell me how you'll take this at home.”
“Do you understand how you'll take this medication at home?”
“Show me how you'll set up your pill box for the coming week.”
“Do you have any questions about how you'll take this at home?”
questions.rationale:
The teach-back method asks the client to describe the main points in the client's own words. Framing it as checking the nurse's explanation keeps it from feeling like a test.

"Show me how you'll set up your pill box" isn't the right answer: it asks for action, but it's a return demonstration of a different skill, and it doesn't show the client knows the schedule's reasons and timing. "Do you understand?" and "Any questions?" invite a simple yes or no, which many clients answer politely without understanding.

Takeaway: Teach-back asks the client to explain in their own words; avoid yes-or-no checks like "Do you understand?"

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching a client about a newly prescribed diuretic and pauses for teach-back. The client says, “I'll take it at bedtime so it can work while I sleep.” Which action should the nurse take next?
options: Move to the next topic, and review the timing at the end
Write the correct timing on the client's handout for home
Note the error, and plan to reteach it at the next visit
Clarify the timing now, then ask the client to explain it again
questions.rationale:
If the client misstates information during teach-back, the nurse clarifies the confusion before moving to the next topic, then has the client explain it again. A diuretic at bedtime causes nighttime urination, broken sleep, and fall risk.

Reviewing the timing at the end isn't the right answer: the nurse does recap the whole session at the end, but leaving the error uncorrected lets it settle in and confuse later topics. Writing it on the handout doesn't confirm understanding, and waiting for the next visit sends the client home with the wrong plan.

Takeaway: When teach-back reveals an error, correct it right then and check again before going on.

questions.stem: A nurse has taught a client four topics before discharge, using teach-back after each one. Which action should the nurse take next?
options: Give the client handouts on the four topics and end the session
Ask the client to explain the main points of the whole session
Ask the client to rate his understanding on a scale of 1 to 10
Document that the teaching was completed and understood
questions.rationale:
After all the topics are taught, the nurse asks the client to explain the major points from the entire session once more. This checks that the pieces fit together and were retained.

Documenting that teaching was understood isn't the right answer: each topic was checked, but the final teach-back of the whole session hasn't been done. Handouts are a good supplement, not the final check, and a self-rating doesn't show what the client actually knows.

Takeaway: Use teach-back after each topic and again for the whole session at the end.

questions.stem: A nurse is documenting a teaching session with a client who has a new prescription for an inhaler. Which information should the nurse include?
options: The client's response to the teaching
The learning needs that were identified
The plan for further teaching
The nurse's opinion of the client's attitude
The materials given to the client
